en: One should meditate upon it as "the Self" alone; by seeking that, everything would be sought. That very reality of the Self must be sought because it is dearer than all else.
"He knew only the Self as 'I am Brahman'"—thus, the single reality of the Self is the object of knowledge (*vidyā*).
But he who is the object of the perception of duality thinks, "He is one and I am another"; "he does not know," for that is the object of ignorance (*avidyā*).

"‘It should be viewed as one alone’; ‘He goes from death to death who perceives here as if there were multiplicity’"—by such passages, the two distinct domains of knowledge (*vidyā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*) are presented in all the Upaniṣads. Among these, the entire domain of ignorance has been explained, through the application of specific distinctions between means and ends, up until the conclusion of the third chapter. And that entire explained domain of ignorance is of two kinds: the internal vital breath (*prāṇa*), which is the supporter like the pillars of a house, and the immortal light, which is the illuminator.

And the external [body], characterized by its effects, non-luminous, subject to arising and passing away, comparable to grass, straw, and clay, and mortal like a house—this is what is denoted by the word "satya" (truth); it is concluded that the vital breath (*prāṇa*), denoted by the word "amṛta" (immortal), is concealed within it.
And that very same *prāṇa* is extended in manifold ways according to the various distinctions of external substrates.
The single vital breath (*prāṇa*) is called the one God.

Its external aggregate (*piṇḍa*), which is one and common to all— consisting of the Virāj, Vaiśvānara, the Self, the Person-shaped Prajāpati, Ka, Hiraṇyagarbha, and so forth— is designated by these terms primarily denoting the aggregate,
and possesses the instruments (*karaṇa*) such as the sun and other organs divided [into their respective functions].

Brahman is both one and many, and it is only this much; there is nothing beyond this. And [the Brahman] which is complete within each individual distinction of bodies—being conscious, an agent, and an enjoyer—is presented as the speaker, Gārgya the Brāhmaṇa, who has approached [this view] by taking that which is merely the object of ignorance to be the Self;
while his listener, Ajātaśatru, possesses a vision of the Self that is the opposite of that.

For in this way, a subject matter presented in the form of prima facie arguments (*pūrvapakṣa*), established conclusions (*siddhānta*), and illustrative narratives (*ākhyāyikā*) comes under the control of the listener's mind;

for otherwise, like a treatise on logic (*tarkaśāstra*), it would be difficult to comprehend when presented through sentences that merely follow the literal meaning, because the reality (*vastu*) is extremely subtle.

Thus, in the *Kaṭhaka*, by such passages as "He who is not obtained even for hearing by many," it is explained in detail how [the Self] is accessible to the intellect of the gods whose minds are well-purified, yet inaccessible to those whose intellects grasp only generalities.
This has been demonstrated:
"A person who has a teacher knows" and "From the teacher alone comes knowledge," as stated in the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad*;
and "The wise who have seen reality will instruct you in knowledge," as stated in the *Bhagavad Gītā*.

Moreover, even here, [the author] will describe the extreme profundity of Brahman with great intensity through the dialogue between Śākalya and Yājñavalkya; therefore, this undertaking is indeed appropriate, being formulated in the form of a narrative to present the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) and the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) for the purpose of establishing the subject matter.
It also serves the purpose of instructing on the rules of conduct (*ācāra-vidhi*); thus, the meaning is understood by following the narrative of Vṛddhaśloka and Vatkṛśoka, who possess such conduct.

The narrative is intended to exclude the notion that [Brahman] can be grasped by mere logic, as evidenced by the Śruti and Smṛti passages: “This wisdom is not to be attained through reasoning” and “not for one consumed by the science of logic.
Furthermore, the meaning of the narrative is that faith (*śraddhā*) is the supreme means for the realization of Brahman.
Indeed, the extreme devotion of Gārgya and Ajātaśatru is clearly observed within this narrative.
And there is a Smṛti text: "The man of faith attains knowledge. Now, Gārgya Dṛptabālāki was a learned man of great erudition.
He said to Ajātaśatru, the King of Kāśī: "I shall tell you about Brahman.
Ajātaśatru replied: "We shall give a thousand [cows] for this speech; indeed, people run about crying, 'Janaka! Janaka! (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.1.1).

In this regard, the proponent of the prima facie view is Bālāki, the son of Balākā, who is arrogant because he possesses knowledge of Brahman that pertains to the sphere of ignorance. He is "arrogant" (dṛpta) because he is conceited due to his [erroneous] knowledge of Brahman. He is a "Bālāki" because he is the offspring of Balākā.
The particle *ha* in the narrative signifies traditional report (*aitihya*).
He is "learned" (*anūcāna*), meaning one capable of reciting the Vedas and one whose speech is eloquent and well-versed.
Gārgya, the son of Gonnata, lived at a certain time;
he, having approached Ajātaśatru—the King of Kāśī named Ajātaśatru—said: "I shall tell you about Brahman; I shall speak of Brahman to you."
Thus addressed, Ajātaśatru said: "I shall give a thousand cows for these words which you have spoken to me—'I will tell you Brahman.
The intention is that the gift of a thousand cows is the sole motive [for speaking].
Why is it not required that the actual telling of Brahman itself be the motive for giving the thousand?
Is it not the case that the phrase "I shall tell you Brahman" requires this very speech as its instrument?
To this it is replied: because the Śruti itself expresses the king's intention by repeating two words in these two sentences—"Janaka is the giver, Janaka is the listener"—repeating "Janaka, Janaka.
The word *vai* is used for the purpose of indicating what is well-known.
"Janaka is one who desires to give; Janaka is one who desires to hear. Thus, people desiring to hear the Brahman, desiring to speak it, and desiring to grasp the Lord run toward and approach [him].
Therefore, you have conceived all of that even in me. //1//
When the king had thus become attentive and was facing him,
Gārgya said: "That very person who is there in the sun— that is the one I venerate as Brahman."
Ajātaśatru said: "Do not converse with me about him!

I meditate upon him as the one who stands over all beings, the head, the king. He who meditates upon him thus becomes one who stands over all beings, the head, the king. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.1.2)

Gārgya said: "That very one who is the single presiding deity (abhimānin) in the sun and in the eye, who has entered here into the heart through the door of the eye and remains established [there] with the thought, 'I am the enjoyer and the doer'—it is him alone that I perceive as Brahman; I meditate upon him within this aggregate of causes and effects."
"Therefore, I shall tell you about that Person, Brahman; meditate upon Him.

Being thus addressed, Ajātaśatru replied, warding him off with his hand, "Not me! Not me!"—meaning, "Do not speak to me regarding this Brahman to be known"; the double usage of "not me" is for the sake of emphasis.
Since the object of consciousness is thus the same for both of us, we would be refuted by you who represent us as if we were ignorant;
therefore, do not converse with me regarding this Brahman— do not engage in discussion on this matter—
if you know something else.
Therefore, you ought to speak of that Brahman which is not already known to me.
Now, if you think, "You know only Brahman in its general sense, but not its specific attributes, meditations, and fruits," that is not how it should be considered.

For I know all this that you say. How so? You are *atiṣṭhāḥ*—you stand transcending all beings (*atītya bhūtāni tiṣṭhasi*), hence you are *atiṣṭhāḥ*. And you are the head, the summit, and the king of all beings; you are *vai-rājā* because you are endowed with splendor and majesty.

"Brahman, distinguished by these attributes, is the agent and the enjoyer within this aggregate of the body and the organs; thus, I meditate upon Him. The fruit for one who meditates upon Him with such distinctions is likewise: "He who meditates upon Him in this way becomes pre-eminent, the head and king of all beings.
For indeed, the fruit corresponds exactly to the qualities of the object of meditation.
"For in whatever way one worships it, that alone one becomes," according to the Śruti. //2//
When the Brahman in the sun had been rejected by Ajātaśatru through his counter-argument, Gārgya proceeded to another Brahman in the moon.
Gārgya said: "That very person who is there in the moon—that is the one I venerate as Brahman."
Ajātaśatru said: "Do not converse with me about him!
I meditate upon him as the Great One, clad in white garments, King Soma.
He who meditates upon him thus has [the Soma] pressed and being pressed for him day after day."
His food is never exhausted.
He who is that single Puruṣa in the moon and in the mind—the enjoyer and the agent—is described by the same qualifiers as before:
he is *bṛhan*, meaning great; and he is *pāṇḍaravāsas*, one whose garment (*vāsa*) is white (*pāṇḍara* or *śukla*).
This is because the vital breath (*prāṇa*), which identifies with the moon, lacks a physical body.
King Soma is the Moon; and that which, having become food, is pressed as a creeper in the sacrifice—
unifying these two, I worship this very one as Brahman.

For one who meditates upon [the Self] possessing the qualities as described, day after day Soma is pressed for him in the primary sacrifice (prakṛti-yajña), and it is "well-pressed" (prasuta)— meaning it is excellently pressed— in the modified sacrifice (vikṛti-yajña); the meaning is that he possesses the capacity to perform both types of sacrifices.
And the food of one who meditates upon the Self as consisting of food is not exhausted. //3//
Gārgya said: "The person who is there in lightning—that very one I venerate as Brahman.
Ajātaśatru said: "Do not converse with me about him."
"Or, I meditate upon him as 'the radiant one.
He who meditates upon him thus becomes radiant, and his offspring become radiant. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.1.4)
Likewise, there is one deity in lightning, in the skin, and in the heart;
"the radiant one" is the qualification, and its fruit is this: he becomes radiant, and his offspring become radiant.
Because of the acceptance of the multiplicity of lightnings, there is an abundance of results for both oneself and one's progeny. //4//
Gārgya said: "The person who is right here in space—that is the one I venerate as Brahman.
Ajātaśatru said: "Do not talk to me about him!"
"Or, 'The Full, the Non-moving'—this is how I worship it.
He who worships it thus is filled with offspring and cattle; his progeny does not perish from this world. (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.1.5)
Likewise, there is one deity in the ether, in the ether of the heart, and in the heart.
There are two qualifiers: "full" (*pūrṇam*) and "unmoving" (*apravarti*).
This is the result of the qualifier "fullness": one is filled with offspring and cattle.
The fruit of the qualification "non-proceeding" is that his progeny does not turn back from this world; that is, there is no interruption in the lineage of his offspring. //5//
Gārgya said: "The person who is here in the wind—that very one I worship as Brahman.
Ajātaśatru said: "Do not converse with me about him."
"I meditate upon him as Indra Vaikuṇṭha, the unconquered army. He who meditates upon him thus becomes victorious, unconquered, and a conqueror of others' forces.
Likewise, there is one deity in the wind, in the vital breath (prāṇa), and in the heart;
her qualification is that she is Indra, the Supreme Lord,
Vaikuṇṭha, the invincible.
The army has never before been defeated by others, for it is renowned as a host of Maruts.

Furthermore, the fruit of its service is that the victorious one—being by nature a conqueror—is "unconquerable" (aparājiṣṇu), meaning he is not one whose character can be overcome by others; rather, he is a "vanquisher of those who stand apart," meaning he is one whose habit is to defeat adversaries. //6//
Gārgya said: "The person who is here in the fire—that very one I venerate as Brahman.
Ajātaśatru said: "Do not converse with me about him."
"Or rather, I meditate upon him as 'the overcomer of poison.
He who meditates upon him thus becomes an overcomer of poison; his offspring also become overcomers of poison. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.1.7)
In fire, speech, and the heart, there is one deity.
Its qualification is "viṣāsahi," meaning one who endures others.
Due to the multiplicity of fires, there is a multiplicity of fruits, as previously explained. //7//
Gārgya said: "The person who is here in the waters—that very one I venerate as Brahman.
Ajātaśatru said: "Do not converse with me about him."
"Or, 'He is handsome; I shall worship him as such. He who worships him in this way, indeed, approaches only what is handsome and not what is unhandsome;
moreover, a handsome son is born from him. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.1.8)
In the waters, in the semen, and in the heart, there is one deity.

Its qualification is "pratirūpaḥ," meaning "anurūpaḥ" (conformable), that is to say, not contrary to the Śruti and Smṛti. As for the result: "pratirūpam" means exactly in accordance with the injunctions of the Śruti and Smṛti; such [a person] approaches and attains this [deity].
It is not contrary [to its cause], and furthermore, something of that very same kind arises from it. //8//
Gārgya said: "The person who is here in the mirror—that very one I venerate as Brahman.
Ajātaśatru said: "Do not converse with me about him."
"I meditate upon him as the Radiant," he said. "He who meditates upon him thus becomes radiant;
his offspring, too, become radiant."
Moreover, he outshines all those with whom he comes into contact.
In a mirror whose nature is clarity, in other [reflective surfaces] such as a sword and so forth, and in the heart whose nature is the purity of the being, there is a single deity;
its qualification is "radiant," meaning its nature is luminosity,
and that very [luminosity] is the fruit.
Due to the abundance of the support for the *rocanā*, there is an abundance of the fruit. //9//
Gārgya said: "The person who is this shadow that follows behind one as they walk—that very one, I worship as Brahman.
Ajātaśatru said: "Do not converse with me about him."
"Verily, I meditate upon him as 'Asu' (Life-breath)," he said.
"He who meditates upon him thus reaches a full span of life in this world;
his vital breath does not leave him before the appointed time."
Regarding the sound that follows one who is going or moving behind from the rear, and which internally is the vital breath (*prāṇa*)— the cause of life— he speaks by identifying these two as one;
"vitality" (*asu*) is the vital breath, the cause of life, which is its quality.
The fruit is that one attains the full span of life in this world—that is, the lifespan acquired through karma.
Even when he is afflicted by diseases and other ailments prior to the time delimited by the fruit of his karma, the vital breath (prāṇa) does not abandon him. //10//
Gārgya said: "The person who is here in the quarters—him indeed I worship as Brahman.
Ajātaśatru said: "Do not converse with me about him."
"Or, 'I worship him as the Second who never departs. He who worships him thus becomes possessed of a companion; his group is not severed from him. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.1.11)
In the quarters, in the ears, and in the heart, there is one deity—the two Aśvin gods—whose nature is inseparable.

Its quality is being dual, being non-separate, and mutual inseparability, because the quarters and the Aśvins possess such a characteristic. And that itself is the fruit for the worshiper: the non-interruption of his community and the state of having a companion. //11//
Gārgya said: "This very person who consists of shadow—that is the one I venerate as Brahman.
Ajātaśatru said: "Do not talk to me about him!"
"Or, I meditate upon this as Death," he said.
He who meditates upon it thus reaches the full span of life in this world;
death does not come to him before his time.
In the shadow—externally in darkness and internally in ignorance characterized by obscuration—and in the heart, there is one deity;
its qualification is "death.
The result is entirely as before.
The distinction is the absence of affliction by disease and so forth due to the non-arrival of death. //12//
Gārgya said: "The person who is here in the self—that very one I worship as Brahman.
Ajātaśatru said: "Do not converse with me about that one."
"I worship him as the Embodied One," he said.
"He who worships him thus becomes embodied; his offspring become embodied."
Gārgya remained silent.
In the self (ātman), in Prajāpati, in the intellect (buddhi), and in the heart, there is one deity.
Her qualifying attributes are "possessing a self" (ātmanvī) and "self-possessed" (ātmavān).
The fruit [of this knowledge] is that one becomes "possessing a self" and indeed becomes "self-possessed."
One whose offspring becomes self-disciplined—this is the distinction, namely that because of the abundance of intelligence, there is the accomplishment [of virtue] among one's progeny.

Since he himself had already understood [these], Gārgya, having thus been rejected step by step regarding those Brahman-entities, his knowledge of Brahman being exhausted and unable to produce a further response, sat silent with his head bowed down. //13//

Having observed him in such a state, Ajātaśatru said to Gārgya: "Is this all? "This is all," he replied. "Is this all? "This is all. "Then, my dear, you have indeed reached the limit of knowledge; however, as for me, I shall tell you about it. Then, taking Gārgya by the hand, he went forth. They came to a person who was sleeping. He addressed him by these names: "O great one! O Vaśa! O Śyeta! O Māṇavaka! But he did not rise at all. Then, pushing him with his hand, he woke him up. Only then did he arise. 2,1.14. Then Ajātaśatru said to Gārgya: "Where was this person here when he was thus asleep? And from where did he come back? Gārgya did not know this. Then Ajātaśatru said: "My dear, it is when this person here has thus fallen asleep—that is, when he has become unified (ekībhūta)—and has gone to rest in his own light, that he does not perceive any external desires or see any external forms. At that time, he becomes this very self (ātman), which consists of pure bliss (ānanda-maya). When he comes out from there again, he perceives desires and sees forms. My dear, it is like this: just as a large fish swims along both banks of a river, the near and the far, so too, my dear, this person here moves along both these states while awake—the state of this world and the state of the other world. My dear, it is like this: just as a falcon or some other bird, having flown around in the sky and becoming weary, folds its wings and dives headlong toward its nest, so too, my dear, this person here, running around as long as he is pursued by what is desirable, becomes weary; he then turns away from desires and reaches his own self. As soon as he attains this self, he thinks: 'I am indeed this—this is my world, and in this world I have all my desires fulfilled. This is his complete fulfillment of all desires. This is his second state of being, in which his desire is for the Self alone, and in which, having obtained all desires, he is satisfied and free from sorrow. When he is thus unified and has gone to rest in his own light, he does not perceive any external desires or see any external forms. At that time, he becomes this very self, which consists of pure bliss. When he comes out from there again, he perceives desires and sees forms. My dear, it is like this: just as a cart, yoked to horses and driven by a driver, goes forward, so too, my dear, this body is yoked to the horses of the vital breaths (prāṇas) and driven by the driver that is the mind (manas). My dear, it is like this: just as when a king is about to set out, the officers of his army assemble around him from all sides, so too, my dear, when this person here departs from this body, all the vital functions (prāṇas) gather around him. "Is it known only this much? "It is not known by this much alone.
Gārgya said, "Let me come to you as a pupil."
Ajātaśatru said: "Is it only this much?"—
that is, "Has Brahman been fully known only to this extent, or is there something more?"
The other said, "Is it only that much?
Ajātaśatru replied, "By knowing only this much, Brahman is not truly known;
why are you so proud? I shall tell you about Brahman."
Is it that what has been known thus far does not truly become known?
To this it is replied: No;

nor can it be understood that these sentences are merely *arthavādas* (eulogistic statements), for each instruction regarding meditation (*upāsana*) is observed to have as its purpose the enjoining of something previously unknown—such as the passage beginning, “He is the support of all beings.”
And corresponding fruits are heard of everywhere as being distributed;
this would be inconsistent if [the passage] were merely an explanatory eulogy (*arthavāda*).
How then is it not understood by this much?
This is not a fault,
because it depends on the person qualified [for instruction].
For Gārgya set out to instruct Ajātaśatru, who was desirous of hearing, regarding Brahman as the primary object of knowledge.

It is entirely appropriate for Ajātaśatru, the foremost knower of Brahman, to say to Gārgya, the foremost knower of Brahman: "You do not know that supreme Brahman about which you have set out to speak.
For if even the knowledge of the non-supreme Brahman were to be rejected, then he would not have said, "So far [you have taught me]."
One should say, "Nothing at all has been known by you"; one should say, "Nothing at all has been known by you.
Therefore, there are only these many Brahmas within the domain of ignorance.
Furthermore, since the knowledge of the Supreme Brahman is attained through these very doors of cognition, it is entirely appropriate to say, "By this much, It has not been known.
That these [elements] possess the nature of being objects of knowledge and consist of name, form, and action within the sphere of ignorance was demonstrated in the third chapter.
Therefore, by saying, "It is not known by this much alone," it is shown that there is further Brahman to be known.

And since that must not be told to one who has not approached [as a disciple], Gārgya, knowing the rules of proper conduct, said of his own accord: "I shall approach you"—that is, I shall go to you as another disciple would go to a teacher. //14//
Ajātaśatru said: "It would be contrary to the natural order for a Brahmin to approach a Kṣatriya thinking, 'He will tell me the Brahman.
Nevertheless, I shall indeed make it known to you."
Taking him by the hand, he stood up.
They two went to a man who was asleep.
He addressed him with these names: "O Great One! O White-Robed One! O Soma! O King!"
He did not rise;
he woke him by pressing him with his hand, and then he rose. (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.1.15)
Ajātaśatru said: "This is contrary and inverted.

What is it? That a Brāhmaṇa, being authorized as a teacher of the highest caste, should approach a Kṣatriya—who by nature is not a teacher—in the manner of a disciple, thinking, 'He will teach me the Brahman.
This is forbidden in the treatises on the rules of conduct."
Therefore, remain right here as my teacher. I myself shall inform you about that which, when known, Brahman becomes known—that primary Brahman which is to be realized.
Observing Gārgya with embarrassment, [Ajātaśatru] took him by the hand to inspire confidence and rose up.

Gārgya and Ajātaśatru went to a certain place in the vicinity of the royal palace where a man was sleeping. Having reached that sleeping man, Gārgya addressed him by these names: “O Great One! O White-robed One! O Soma! O King! Though thus addressed, the sleeping man did not rise.
Pressing him repeatedly with his hand and waking him up, he caused him to regain consciousness;
thereby he rose.
Therefore, he who was intended by Gārgya is not the agent, the enjoyer, or Brahman in this body.

But how is it understood that, by means of the sleeping man’s departure, his awakening, and his failure to rise upon being addressed, the non-Brahmanhood of the Brahman as conceived by Gārgya is made known? Just as the person intended by Gārgya— the agent and enjoyer who is present within the organs during the waking state— is Brahman, so too the person intended by Ajātaśatru, who is its master like a king among his servants, is likewise present [within them].

However, the reason for determining the distinction between the servant and the master intended by Gārgya and Ajātaśatru is such that their specific characteristics have not been ascertained due to their being intermingled;
namely, that the enjoyer is indeed the seer and not the seen,
whereas the non-enjoyer is indeed the seen and not the seer.

Since both of these [states] are intermingled here, it is impossible to demonstrate them by distinguishing them; therefore, there is the approach to the sleeping man. Now, one might object: "Even when a man is asleep, if addressed by specific names, only the enjoyer (the self) would respond, not the non-enjoyer; thus, no certain conclusion could be reached.

This is not so, because the specific nature intended by Gārgya has already been determined: it is that immortal Self, the vital breath (*prāṇa*), which is veiled by truth, which does not set while speech and the other organs set.
He whose body is water, who is clad in white garments,
who is great because he has no rival,
and who is King Soma consisting of sixteen parts— [he is that].
He remains with his own nature unextinguished, exactly as he was previously known, mounted upon his own activity;
nor is any other activity intended by Gārgya at that time, for it would be contradictory to him.
Therefore, he must be awakened by being addressed by his own names.
And yet he did not wake up.
Therefore, by the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), it follows that Brahman, as intended by Gārgya, is not the enjoyer.
If its essential nature were that of an enjoyer, it would surely have enjoyed its own object once it had reached it.

For fire, which possesses the nature of a burner and the nature of an illuminator, does not fail to burn combustible things such as grass and brushwood, nor does it fail to illuminate what is to be illuminated,
once it has reached its own object; provided, however, that it does indeed burn or illuminate its own reached object.
It is not determined that "this fire neither burns nor illuminates.

Likewise, if this Prāṇa intended by Gārgya— whose nature is that of a perceiver of objects such as sound that have come into contact— is indeed so, then he would perceive his own object, namely the words "Bṛhat," "Pāṇḍaravāsa," and so forth, just as fire invariably burns and illuminates the grass, reeds, and other things that come into contact with it.
Therefore, it is determined that because [the self] does not perceive the sounds and other objects when they have been reached, its nature is that of a non-experiencer;
for whatever nature is ascertained to belong to something, that thing never deviates from it at any time.
Therefore, it is established that the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is not the enjoyer.

If it is argued that there is no awakening because of the failure to grasp the connection [between the name and the person] due to the lack of distinction in the names used for addressing, this might be so:
just as when many people are sitting together, one fails to grasp the connection through the specific distinction of one's own name and thinks, "He is addressing me."

If it is argued that even while hearing and being specifically addressed, one does not understand—just as the vital breath (*prāṇa*) does not grasp the word used for the purpose of addressing because it has not grasped the relationship [between name and bearer], such as "O Bṛhan" and so forth, and not merely because of a lack of consciousness; [Response: No. For even though the vital breath does not understand, it nevertheless moves toward the sound of the address. But the other [the person] does not move toward it at all. Therefore, this [non-understanding] is due to a lack of consciousness, and not to a failure to grasp the relationship [between name and bearer]. Furthermore, if the vital breath were not conscious, it would not be possible for it to be addressed by means of names such as "Bṛhan. Thus, the vital breath is indeed conscious. Moreover, if the vital breath were not conscious, then since it is the agent of speech, it would follow that it is the speaker, and consequently, the knower would be different from the speaker. But this is not accepted. Therefore, the vital breath is conscious. Furthermore, if the vital breath were not conscious, then when it departs, the body would not fall down lifeless, just as a wooden log does not fall when a non-conscious axe is removed. But since it falls, the vital breath is conscious. And if it were not conscious, it could not be the agent of departure, just as a wooden log cannot be the agent of departure. But since it is the agent of departure, the vital breath is conscious. Furthermore, if the vital breath were not conscious, then upon its departure, the body would not be seen to become cold, just as a wooden log does not become cold when a non-conscious axe is removed. But since it becomes cold, the vital breath is conscious. And if it were not conscious, it could not be the cause of coldness, just as a wooden log is not the cause of coldness when a non-conscious axe is removed. But since it is the cause of coldness, the vital breath is conscious. Moreover, if the vital breath were not conscious, then when it departs, the body would not be seen to become devoid of warmth, just as a wooden log does not become devoid of warmth when a non-conscious axe is removed. But since it becomes devoid of warmth, the vital breath is conscious. And if it were not conscious, it could not be the cause of the loss of warmth, just as a wooden log is not the cause of the loss of warmth when a non-conscious axe is removed. But since it is the cause of the loss of warmth, the vital breath is conscious. Furthermore, if the vital breath were not conscious, then when it departs, the body would not be seen to become devoid of movement, just as a wooden log does not become devoid of movement when a non-conscious axe is removed. But since it becomes devoid of movement, the vital breath is conscious. And if it were not conscious, it could not be the cause of movement, just as a wooden log is not the cause of movement when a non-conscious axe is removed. But since it is the cause of movement, the vital breath is conscious. Moreover, if the vital breath were not conscious, then when it departs, the body would not be seen to become devoid of consciousness, just as a wooden log does not become devoid of consciousness when a non-conscious axe is removed. But since it becomes devoid of consciousness, the vital breath is conscious. And if it were not conscious, it could not be the cause of consciousness, just as a wooden log is not the cause of consciousness when a non-conscious axe is removed. But since it is the cause of consciousness, the vital breath is conscious. Furthermore, if the vital breath were not conscious, then when it departs, the body would not be seen to become devoid of life, just as a wooden log does not become devoid of life when a non-conscious axe is removed. But since it becomes devoid of life, the vital breath is conscious. And if it were not conscious, it could not be the cause of life, just as a wooden log is not the cause of life when a non-conscious axe is removed. But since it is the cause of life, the vital breath is conscious. Moreover, if the vital breath were not conscious, then when it departs, the body would not be seen to become devoid of all functions, just as a wooden log does not become devoid of all functions when a non-conscious axe is removed. But since it becomes devoid of all functions, the vital breath is conscious. And if it were not conscious, it could not be the cause of the cessation of all functions, just as a wooden log is not the cause of the cessation of all functions when a non-conscious axe is removed. But since it is the cause of the cessation of all functions, the vital breath is conscious. Furthermore, if the vital breath were not conscious, then when it departs, the body would not be seen to become devoid of all light, just as a wooden log does not become devoid of all light when a non-conscious axe is removed. But since it becomes devoid of all light, the vital breath is conscious. And if it were not conscious, it could not be the cause of the loss of all light, just as a wooden log is not the cause of the loss of all light when a non-conscious axe is removed. But since it is the cause of the loss of all light, the vital breath is conscious. Moreover, if the vital breath were not conscious, then when it departs, the body would not be seen to become devoid of all power, just as a wooden log does not become devoid of all power when a non-conscious axe is removed. But since it becomes devoid of all power, the vital breath is conscious. And if it were not conscious, it could not be the cause of the loss of all power, just as a wooden log is not the cause of the loss of all power when a non-conscious axe is removed. But since it is the cause of the loss of all power, the vital breath is conscious. Furthermore, if the vital breath were not conscious, then when it departs, the body would not be seen to become devoid of all vitality, just as a wooden log does not become devoid of all vitality when a non-conscious axe is removed. But since it becomes devoid of all vitality, the vital breath is conscious. And if it were not conscious, it could not be the cause of the loss of all vitality, just as a wooden log is not the cause of the loss of all vitality when a non-conscious axe is removed. But since it is the cause of the loss of all vitality, the vital breath is conscious. Moreover, if the vital breath were not conscious, then when it departs, the body would not be seen to become devoid of all support, just as a wooden log does not become devoid of all support when a non-conscious axe is removed. But since it becomes devoid of all support, the vital breath is conscious. And if it were not conscious, it could not be the cause of the loss of all support, just as a wooden log is not the cause of the loss of all support when a non-conscious axe is removed. But since it is the cause of the loss of all support, the vital breath is conscious. Furthermore, if the vital breath were not conscious, then when it departs, the body would not be seen to become devoid of all essence, just as a wooden log does not become devoid of all essence when a non-conscious axe is removed. But since it becomes devoid of all essence, the vital breath is conscious. And if it were not conscious, it could not be the cause of the loss of all essence, just as a wooden log is not the cause of the loss of all essence when a non-conscious axe is removed. But since it is the cause of the loss of all essence, the vital breath is conscious. Moreover, if the vital breath were not conscious, then when it departs, the body would not be seen to become devoid of all integrity, just as a wooden log does not become devoid of all integrity when a non-conscious axe is removed. But since it becomes devoid of all integrity, the vital breath is conscious. And if it were not conscious, it could not be the cause of the loss of all integrity, just as a wooden log is not the cause of the loss of all integrity when a non-conscious axe is removed. But since it is the cause of the loss of all integrity, the vital breath is conscious. Furthermore, if the vital breath were not conscious, then when it departs, the body would not be seen to become devoid of all stability, just as a wooden log does not become devoid of all stability when a non-conscious axe is removed. But since it becomes devoid of all stability, the vital breath is conscious. And if it were not conscious, it could not be the cause of the loss of all stability, just as a wooden log is not the cause of the loss of all stability when a non-conscious axe is removed. But since it is the cause of the loss of all stability, the vital breath is conscious. Moreover, if the vital breath were not conscious, then when it departs, the body would not be seen to become devoid of all sovereignty, just as a wooden log does not become devoid of all sovereignty when a non-conscious axe is removed. But since it becomes devoid of all sovereignty, the vital breath is conscious. And if it were not conscious, it could not be the cause of the loss of all sovereignty, just as a wooden log is not the cause of the loss of all sovereignty when a non-conscious axe is removed. But since it is the cause of the loss of all sovereignty, the vital breath is conscious. Furthermore, if the vital breath were not conscious,
No; for if a deity were accepted [as the eater], grasping would be untenable.

For one who accepts that the deity presiding over the moon and so forth is the internal vital breath (*prāṇa*) as the enjoyer, a connection with a specific name must necessarily be grasped for the sake of conventional usage.
Otherwise, worldly transaction regarding summoning and so forth would be untenable.
If it is argued that even in the view of [the self] being distinct [from the vital breath], it is improper because there is no cognition [of such a self],
then for whomsoever the enjoyer is distinct from the vital breath—

Furthermore, when he is addressed by names such as "Bṛhan" and so forth, it would be logical for him to understand them, since those names— such as "the Great One"— would at that time have him as their referent;
yet he is never observed to understand himself when addressed with words like "the Great One."
If it is argued that, therefore, the failure to understand the address is not a reason for [the Self's] non-enjoyment, we say no;
because for one who possesses such [a body], an identification with merely that much [the vital breath] is untenable.

For one who holds that the enjoyer is distinct from the vital breath, there can be no identification with the deity of the vital breath alone, just as one does not identify with the hand [as the whole person].
Therefore, it is appropriate that there is no recognition when addressed by a name common to all living beings; however, this is not the case when addressed by a name unique to Prāṇa,
because the Self does not identify itself with the nature of a deity.
If it is argued that [the objection] is incorrect because we observe a lack of comprehension even when one's own name is employed:

[we reply that] even when a person in deep sleep is addressed by his worldly name such as Devadatta, that sleeper sometimes does not comprehend; likewise, the vital breath (prāṇa), though being the enjoyer, does not comprehend. If this is your argument?
No, because a distinction between the self and the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is established by their respective states of being asleep and awake.
Due to its state of deep sleep, the self—having ceased its functions because it is swallowed by the vital breath—does not perceive its own name even when it is being uttered.
However, for the vital breath, which is not asleep and is the experiencer, it is not logical that its organs should cease to function or that it should fail to grasp an address.

If it is argued that addressing [the subject] by means of names that are not well-known is improper— since there are indeed well-known names such as "prāṇa" (breath) and so forth pertaining to the vital breaths—
it is improper to set those aside and address it by means of names like "bṛhat" (greatness) and so forth, which are not well-known.
If it is argued that this is because of the exclusion of worldly logic,
and therefore there is no apprehension of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) as being merely the enjoyer, we say:
no, because the purpose is to exclude [the notion of] a deity.

Since the fact that the internal vital breath (*prāṇa*) is not the enjoyer is already established by the mere failure to understand the singular address, the addressing it with names pertaining to the deity Moon is for the purpose of refuting Gārgya’s specific misconception that the deity Moon is the enjoyer in this body;
for it would not have been possible to effect that [refutation] by addressing it with a worldly name.

Because the other organs are swallowed by the vital breath (prāṇa), their activity is untenable, and thus the suspicion that they could be the enjoyers is untenable; furthermore, there is an absence of any other presiding deities.
If it is argued that this is not so, because the distinction between various qualified deities has been shown by the passage beginning with "He stood firm" and ending with "possessing a self"?
No, because in all the Śrutis, that [Self] is admitted to be one with Prāṇa through the illustration of the nave and the spokes;

and because nothing other than Prāṇa is admitted as the enjoyer, as seen in the passage, "It is covered by truth; Prāṇa indeed is the immortal"; and because the oneness of all the gods with Prāṇa alone is established in such passages as, "For he alone is all the gods," and "Which one is the single god? Prāṇa."
Likewise, there can be no suspicion of non-permanence regarding the various instruments [of action],
because— just as in the case of different bodies— the synthesis of memory, cognition, desire, and so forth would be impossible;
for one person does not remember, cognize, desire, or synthesize what was seen by another.
Therefore, the suspicion that there is an enjoyer—whether as distinct from the instruments or as consisting of mere consciousness—is never tenable.
[Objection: Let the aggregate itself be the enjoyer; what is the use of postulating something separate?
No; because a difference is observed upon pressing.

For if the enjoyer were merely the aggregate of the vital breaths and the body, then, since there would be no distinction in being a mere aggregate, there would be no difference in consciousness between one who has been pressed and one who has not been pressed.

However, if the enjoyer is distinct from the aggregate, then—due to the multiplicity of specific relations with the aggregate and due to the occurrence of distinctions in the fruits of karma (such as pleasure, pain, and delusion, or superior, middling, and inferior)—it is logical that there should be a difference in sensation caused by pressing or not pressing.
A distinction is appropriate;
however, in the case of a mere aggregate, a distinction is not appropriate because the differentiation between connection, action, and fruit would be untenable.
Likewise, [a distinction] is also produced by the sharpness or dullness of the auditory faculty and so forth.
And there is this distinction: because King Ajātaśatru awakened the sleeping man—who did not wake at the mere touch—by repeatedly pressing him with his hand;

therefore, it is established that he who was awakened by the pressing, who was as if blazing, as if throbbing, as if arrived from somewhere, and who brought about a transformation in the body by endowing it with specific qualities such as consciousness, effort, and form, is someone other than the Brahman favored by Gārgya.
Furthermore, because it is composite, the existence of the vital breath (prāṇa) as subserving another is established.
We have already stated that the vital breath, acting as the internal support for the body—just as pillars and other elements are for a house—is itself composed of the body and its constituents.
This is also like the spokes and the rim [of a wheel].

And because it is said, "In this [Self], which stands in the place of the navel, everything [rests]," we have understood that, like a house and so forth, it is a collection of its own parts that exists for the sake of an object distinct from itself. For the parts of a house—such as pillars, walls, grass, and wood—possess their existence independently of their own birth, growth, decay, destruction, name, form, function, and qualities; rather, they exist for the sake of the seer, the hearer, the thinker, and the knower who perceive those objects.

Having observed this, we consider that— just as in the case of the body and its constituent parts— it must be so for the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and the rest, as well as for their respective aggregates, that they exist for the sake of a seer, hearer, thinker, and knower who has attained its own existence independently of the self-nature, birth, growth, decay, destruction, name, form, and functional properties of those [parts] and their objects.

If it is argued that because the deity possesses consciousness, it is equal [to the individual soul] and thus cannot attain the status of being subordinate, we reply: the deity's possession of consciousness is accepted because it is seen to be addressed by specific names.
And if it is further argued that since it possesses consciousness, its subordination to another (the individual soul) is untenable due to their equality, we say no;
for it is the deity in its unconditioned, absolute state that is intended to be made known.

For the nature of the self as consisting of action, agent, and fruit is produced by the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) of name and form, and is superimposed by ignorance (avidyā). Caused by that [ignorance], there is the cycle of existence (saṃsāra) for the world, characterized by the conceit of action, agent, and fruit. That [cycle] must be removed by the knowledge of the true nature of the self as devoid of limiting adjuncts; thus, with the desire to make known its true nature, the Upaniṣad begins: "Brahman..."

Having begun with, "I shall tell you," and "It is not known by this much alone," and having concluded with, "This much indeed, my dear, is immortality," there is nothing else stated in the interval that is intended to be expressed.
Therefore, the objection— that because of their equality [with the Self], they cannot attain the status of being subordinate qualities— is out of place.
For the relationship of quality and possessor of qualities exists for the sake of conventional usage only in that which possesses distinctions and is qualified by limiting adjuncts (upādhi),
not in the opposite case; indeed,
it is the indefinable (nirupākhya) that is intended to be made known throughout every Upaniṣad.
This is because of the concluding statement, "Not this, not this.
Therefore, it is established that there exists another, distinct from these [entities] such as the sun which consist of Brahman, namely the one consisting of consciousness (vijñānamaya). //15//
Ajātaśatru said: "When this person, who consists of consciousness, was thus asleep, where had he then been, and from whence did he now return? Gārgya did not know that.

Having thus established the existence of a self distinct [from the body], Ajātaśatru said to Gārgya: "At what time—during which period this person consisting of consciousness (vijñānamaya) was asleep, having fallen into this sleep until the time of waking by the clapping of hands;
*vijñāna* is called the internal organ, the intellect (*buddhi*), because by means of it one cognizes (*vijñāyate*);
*vijñānamaya* means composed of that, or predominantly consisting of that."
What, then, is this "state of being predominant" (*prāyatva*)?
It is the state of being perceived therein, and by that [predominance], both the state of being perceived and the state of being a perceiver [are indicated].
But how, given that the suffix *mayaṭ* has multiple meanings, is it understood specifically in the sense of "predominance"?

Because in passages such as, “This very Self is Brahman, consisting of knowledge, consisting of mind,” we observe that the term is used primarily in the sense of "predominance"; because it is not well-known for [the Self] to be a modification of supreme knowledge; because the statement, “He who consists of knowledge,” is a restatement of what is already established; and because the meanings of "parts" or "simile" are impossible here, it follows by the method of elimination that the meaning is indeed "predominance."

Therefore, the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), which consists of volition, conceptualization, and so forth, is composed of that [unmanifested state]. The term "Person" (puruṣa) is used because he dwells within the city (puri śayanāt).

The question, "Where was this [Self] then? is intended to make known its true nature; for prior to awakening, it is desired to demonstrate that the Self possesses a nature contrary to action, agent, and fruit, by means of the absence of all effects.
For indeed, prior to awakening, no effect of action such as pleasure or the like is perceived;
nor is any effect of action such as pleasure or the like perceived prior to awakening.
Therefore, because it is not impelled by action, the very nature of the Self is understood to be such that it existed in that state of being its own nature.

And because the transmigrating being, having fallen away from its own nature, is characterized by a nature different from that [true] nature—it is with this intention that [the Teacher] questions Gārgya, who was lacking in ready wit, in order to stimulate his understanding: "Where did he then abide?
Whence did he come?"
Both of these points ought to have been asked by Gārgya himself;
nevertheless, Ajātaśatru does not remain indifferent because Gārgya did not ask them,
but proceeds with the thought that he must certainly be enlightened.

Because he had promised, "I shall indeed make it known," Gārgya, even while being thus instructed, did not comprehend both that wherein this Self was prior to its awakening and from whence it came when it departed; Gārgya did not know, nor did he understand, how to speak of or to ask about those two things. //16//

Ajātaśatru said: "When this person, who consists of consciousness, was thus asleep— having taken the consciousness of these vital breaths by means of his own consciousness— he lies in that space which is within the heart."
When he grasps those [organs],
then indeed it is called "a person sleeps"; at that time,
the vital breath (prāṇa) alone remains grasped.
Speech is grasped;
the eye is grasped;
the ear is grasped.
The mind was grasped. Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.1.17.

Ajātaśatru spoke thus to convey his intended meaning: "Regarding that which we asked—'When this person consisting of consciousness was asleep here, from where did he come?'—" (Note: The text provided repeats "ya eṣa vijñānamayaḥ puruṣaḥ" twice; the translation reflects the structure of the original while clarifying the intent.)

Listen to that which is being told: at the time when he was thus asleep, [the Self], by means of the consciousness (*vijñāna*)— that is, the specific manifesting cognition residing in the internal organ produced by the nature of the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*)— having taken away the consciousness of these vital breaths (*prāṇas*), such as speech and the rest, meaning having grasped the capacity of speech and the others directed toward their respective objects, [remains].
That which is this space within the middle of the heart— by the word "space" (ākāśa), the Supreme Self alone is meant— it rests in that very Self, in that innate and non-transmigratory space.

It is not merely into space alone, according to the force of another scriptural passage: "Then, my dear, he becomes united with Being. The intention is that, having cast off the specific nature of the self created by the connection with the limiting adjuncts (liṅga-upādhi), he abides in the Self alone, which is undifferentiated and natural.
When it relinquishes its presiding over the body and the senses,
how is it known that it then abides in itself?
By the well-known designation [of the self].
What is this well-known designation?
To this he says: when, at which time, one grasps—that is, takes up—those cognitions of speech and so forth, then at that time this person is said to "sleep";
this name of this person becomes well-known at that time.
Its name is indeed secondary (gauṇa).
Because it goes back into its own very self (svam evātmānam apigacchati), it is called "sleeping" (svapiti).
Through the well-known application of the term "sleeping," the true nature of the Self, which is distinct from the attributes of transmigratory existence (saṃsāra-dharma), is understood.
Anticipating the objection that there is no logical justification for this, he says: "In that regard, at the time of sleep, the vital breath (prāṇa) is indeed withdrawn.
Here, "prāṇa" refers to the olfactory organ, because the context concerns speech and the other [senses].
For when there is a connection with speech and the other senses, its nature as subject to transmigratory existence is indicated because it possesses those as its limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).
And at that time, speech and the others have indeed been withdrawn by him.
How so? "Speech is withdrawn, the eye is withdrawn, the ear is withdrawn, the mind is withdrawn."

Therefore, when speech and the other organs have been withdrawn, since the nature of action, agent, and fruit no longer exists, it is understood that the Self remains established in its own self. //17//

But surely, even in the state of dream, which is characterized by perception, this [self] is seen to possess the attributes of transmigratory existence despite being dissociated from the body and the senses.
And just as in the waking state it is happy, miserable, separated from kinsmen, grieves, and is deluded;
therefore, this [self] possesses the very nature of grief and delusion.
For him, sorrow, delusion, and so forth, as well as pleasure, pain, and the like, are not superimpositions resulting from the error produced by the conjunction of the body and the instruments;
this is because they are not false.
When he moves about in this state of dreaming, these indeed are his worlds.
Then he becomes, as it were, a great king; as it were, a great Brahmin; and he enters, as it were, into various high and low states.

Just as a great king, having taken hold of the people of his realm, moves about in his own territory according to his pleasure, even so this [self], having taken hold of the vital breaths, moves about in its own body according to its pleasure.
When that aforementioned Self moves about—that is, exists—in the state of dreaming, characterized by the vision of dreams, then those worlds are his fruits of action.
What are they? In that state, O Great King, he becomes as if a great king; this world of his is like the status of a great king.
It is not only the state of being a great king that is like waking; likewise, it is not only the state of being a great brahmin,
but also various high and low states— high such as divinity and low such as animalhood.
He encounters both the high and the low;
for his worldly states, such as the status of a great king and so forth, are merely false,
because of the use of the word "as it were" (*iva*) and because of the observation of their variability.

Therefore, one is certainly not connected in a dream with grief, delusion, and so forth, born from separation from kinsmen and the like. Now, just as in the waking state there are worlds that do not deviate from the time of waking,
so too in a dream those worlds— such as being a great king— which exist during the time of the dream and do not deviate from the time of the dream, are indeed one's own self.
"But they are not superimposed by ignorance.

[Objection: But has it not already been demonstrated, by showing the self consisting of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*) as distinct [from the body], that the state of being the agent of actions during the waking state and the state of being a deity are superimposed by ignorance and do not exist in the ultimate sense?
So how can the world of dreams appear as an illustration, as if rising from the dead?

True; it is established by the very logic of demonstrating the existence of a distinct Self that the presentation of the identity with the body, the organs, and the deities within the Self consisting of consciousness—which is actually superimposed by ignorance like the perception of silver in mother-of-pearl—is merely an appearance.
However, the logic was not stated for the purpose of establishing that purity alone;
thus, even though it is unreal, the illustration characterized by the perception of identity with the body, the organs, and the deities in the waking state is brought forward once again.
For every logical argument becomes non-redundant only by depending on some specific qualification.
First of all, the worlds experienced in a dream— such as being a great king and so forth— are not identical with the self,
because one perceives a world that is distinct from the self and serves as its waking counterpart.

Great King, consider first this: while the subjects are asleep in their various quarters, you lie upon your couch, seeing dreams; yet with your senses withdrawn, you perceive yourself as if awake, as if you were that very same great king who has returned to his natural state, traveling on his journey and enjoying pleasures. And there exists no second person other than that great king, endowed with his natural form, wandering through the realm and renowned in the world during the day, who is seen lying upon the couch.
That which this person sees while asleep cannot be a perception of something possessing form and so forth by one whose sense organs have been withdrawn;
nor is it possible for another body, similar to the first, to exist within the body.
For it is indeed for one remaining within the body that there is the vision of dreams.

[Objection: But surely one lying on a couch sees oneself proceeding on a road; thus, he says that one does not see dreams outside [the body]: "That great king, having taken and brought along his subjects—those born in the countryside—and other attendants who serve as the king's implements."
In his own domain, acquired through victory and other means, he may turn about according to his desire— meaning that whatever desire he has,
he turns it according to his wish; in this very same way, this one consisting of consciousness [turns about].
The word "this" (etad) is an adverbial modifier.
Having taken hold of the vital breaths—that is, having withdrawn them from the states of waking—he moves about as he desires within his own body, not outside;
the meaning is that he experiences mental impressions (vāsanās) resembling things previously experienced, which are manifested by desire and past action.

Therefore, it should be understood that just as in a dream the worlds— which are non-existent— appear merely as false superimpositions through the sense of being one's own self, so too it is in the waking state.
Therefore, it is established that the one consisting of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*) is pure, characterized by the absence of action, agent, and fruit;
for worlds characterized as effects and instruments— which consist of action, agent, and fruit— are seen as objects of the seer both in the waking state and likewise in a dream.
Therefore, that seer who consists of consciousness and is pure is distinct from those visible worlds of dream and waking. //18//

In the state of dreaming, which consists of the activity of seeing, because the multitude of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) is the object of perception, it is understood that they are not attributes of the Self; thus, the purity of the Self is established.
In that context, the statement "he moves about according to his desire" describes movement under the influence of desire.
Furthermore, because the relationship between this seer and the seen is considered inherent, impurity is suspected;
therefore, for the sake of its purification, he says:
"Now, when one is in deep sleep..."
When he knows nothing at all,
then those seventy-two thousand channels called *hitā*, which extend from the heart to the pericardium, serve as his path;
having descended through them, he rests in the pericardium.
Just as a young boy, or a great king, or a great Brahmin, having reached the height of bliss, might lie down, even so does he lie here. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.1.19)
Now, when one is in deep sleep— or when one moves about in a dream—

even then this [Self] is indeed pure. Furthermore, when, having abandoned the state of dreaming, one is in deep sleep (*suṣupta*)— that is, well-sleeping— at which time one becomes serene (*samprasāda*) by virtue of one's own essential nature.
When does one become fast asleep?
At what time— meaning, when— at which moment, one knows nothing of anyone, that is to say, one perceives nothing.
Alternatively, it must be supplied [to the text] that "one does not know any other related entity whatsoever, such as sound and so forth"; however,
the former [interpretation] is more logical, because what is intended to be expressed is the absence of specific cognition during sleep.
Thus far, it has been stated that one becomes deeply asleep when there is an absence of specific cognitions.

But by what sequence does one become deeply asleep? It is said: There are channels called "hitā" (the Beneficial); these are vessels consisting of the transformation of the essence of food within the body.
And those are seventy-two thousand—
that is, two thousand in excess of seventy thousand; they are the seventy-two thousand [channels] from the heart— the "heart" being a lump of flesh— from that lotus-shaped lump of flesh.

They call the *purītat* the covering of the heart; the body characterized by that [covering] is what is intended here by the term *purītat*. The meaning is that, pervading the entire body, they proceed outward like the veins on the surface of an ashvattha leaf.
In this context, the heart is the location of the intellect (*buddhi*), which is the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).
The internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*) residing therein are the intellect (*buddhi*) and the others, while the external organs (*bāhyakaraṇa*) are the ears and so forth.

Therefore, by the power of karma, the intellect extends the ears and other organs through those channels— like a fisherman’s net— from their locations such as the ear-cavities, and having extended them, it presides over them during the waking state.
The one consisting of consciousness (vijñānamaya) pervades that [intellect] by means of the manifestation of the radiance of its own self-consciousness;
and at the time of its contraction, it contracts along with it—
this is the sleep of this one consisting of consciousness.
Experience is the perception of the expansion during the waking state;
for it conforms to the nature of the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of the intellect,
just as the reflection of the moon and other objects conforms to the water and other media.
Therefore, following the withdrawal of that waking consciousness through those channels, it "lies" (śete)—that is, it remains—within the body (purītat).
The meaning is that, like a heated iron ball, it exists pervading the body without distinction, as fire pervades its vessel.
Although it abides in its own essential self, it is said to "lie in the body" because it follows the intellect (buddhi) which is itself governed by karma.
For indeed, at the time of deep sleep, there is no connection with the body;
for it will be said: "For then he has crossed beyond all sorrows of the heart.
This state is one free from all the miseries of saṃsāra; regarding this, there is an illustration: "Just as a young boy, or one who is extremely childish..."
Or a great king whose subjects are entirely submissive and who acts according to his word; or a great brahmin who is fully matured and endowed with perfected knowledge and discipline—
having reached and attained that state of bliss, which is called "atighnī" because it exceedingly destroys (han) suffering and is thus a state of supreme joy.
One should lie down or remain standing.
For these [beings], such as children and others, when abiding in their own nature, happiness is well-known in the world as being unsurpassed;
for when they are undergoing transformation, there is suffering, but not by way of their own nature.
Therefore, their state of naturalness (*svābhāvikyavasthā*) is taken as the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) because it is well-known;
their actual sleep is not intended [as the example],
since sleep is what is meant to be the illustrated subject (*dārṣṭāntika*), and because there would otherwise be no distinction.
For only if there were a distinction would there be a difference between the illustrative example (dṛṣṭānta) and the subject of illustration (dārṣṭāntika);
therefore, their sleep is not an appropriate illustration.
It is exactly as this illustration [shows].
"This one consisting of consciousness sleeps on this bed"—here, the word "this" (etad) serves as an adverbial modifier for the action.
Thus, during the time of sleep, he exists in his own natural self, which transcends all the attributes of transmigratory existence. //19//
The answer to the question, "Where was he then? has been stated.
And by this resolution of the question, it is declared that the one consisting of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*) is, by its very nature, pure and non-transmigratory.
This undertaking is for the purpose of answering the question, "From where did this come?
Now, one might object: when someone resides in a certain village or city and goes elsewhere, they go from that very village or city, not from somewhere else.

That being the case, let the question simply be: "Where was it then? Since it is well known that it returned from exactly where it had been and not from elsewhere, the question "From where did it come? is entirely purposeless.
Are you perhaps censuring the Śruti? No.
What then? I wish to hear a different meaning for the second question, and therefore I urge that [the first] is purposeless.
If that is so, why is the sense of an *apādāna* (ablative) not accepted;
for if it were an *apādāna*, there would be a redundancy.
It is not for the sake of another meaning.
Let it then be that the question is for the sake of the cause—[asking] "From where did this come? or "What is the cause of its coming here?
It is not even for the sake of the cause.
Because of the disparity in the responses;
for in the response, the origin of the Self and of the entire world is heard to be like that of sparks from a fire.
Indeed, when sparks fly forth, the fire is not their efficient cause (nimitta), but rather it is their material source (apādāna).
Likewise, the Supreme Self is heard in scripture as the material cause (*apādāna*) of the self consisting of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*), in this passage: "from this self.
Therefore, because of the contradiction with the answer, it is impossible to describe the question "whence? as having the sense of a cause (*nimitta*).
[Objection: But even in the case of the *apādāna* interpretation, the fault of tautology remains exactly the same.
This is not a fault,
because by means of the two questions, what is intended to be expressed is the negation of the nature of action, agent, and fruit with respect to the Self.
For here, the domains of knowledge and ignorance have been presented.
"One should meditate on [the Self] as the Self," "He knew only the Self," and "One should meditate on the Self alone as the world"—these constitute the domain of knowledge (*vidyā*).
Likewise, the domain of ignorance (*avidyā*) consists of fivefold ritual action and its fruit, the three kinds of food, which are of the nature of name, form, and action.
Regarding that, everything that was to be said concerning the domain of ignorance has now been stated.
However, the Self, which is the object of knowledge, was merely introduced and not yet determined.
For the purpose of determining it, [the teacher] began with "I shall tell you of Brahman" and "I shall make it known.
Therefore, that Brahman, which is the object of knowledge, must be made known according to its true nature.
And its true nature is intended here as being devoid of the distinctions of action, agent, and fruit, absolutely pure, and non-dual.
Therefore, two questions corresponding to that [nature] are raised by the Śruti: "Where was this then? and "From whence did it come?
In this context, that wherein something exists is the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), and that which exists is the subject (*adhikartavya*).

Since in the world a distinction between the locus and the one who occupies it is observed, and likewise, that from which something comes is the *apādāna* (ablative point), while he who comes is the agent (*kartṛ*), and is seen to be distinct from that [point]; so too, the notion arises—consistent with worldly experience—that the Self must have existed somewhere else as one thing, or that another has come from somewhere else as another, or that it has been produced by some other distinct instrument. Such is the understanding reached according to worldly analogy.
She is to be turned back by this reply:
"This self was not one thing and another at another time, nor did it come from another; nor does there exist any other means of accomplishment for the self."

What then? It was [dissolved] in its own self alone, according to such scriptural passages as: "He has gone to his own (self)," "Then, my dear, he becomes united with Being," "He is completely embraced by the conscious Self," and "He is established in the Supreme Self."
For this very reason, nothing comes from anything else;
this is demonstrated by the very words "from this Self," because there is no other entity apart from the Self.
Is there not, then, some other entity distinct from the self, such as the vital breath (prāṇa) and so forth?
No; for the vital breath and the rest are produced from that very [self]. How is this so? It is said:
In this regard, there is an illustration:
just as threads emerge from a spider, and just as tiny sparks fly forth from a fire, even so from this Self all vital breaths (prāṇas), all worlds, all deities,
and all beings emerge.
Its secret name (upaniṣad) is "the truth of truth.
The vital breaths (prāṇas) are indeed truth, and he is their truth.
Just as in the world a spider—
a spider being well-known as a single kind of silkworm— might ascend or rise up by means of a thread that is not distinct from its own self;
and in its rising, there is no other separate agent apart from itself.
And just as from a single fire of one form, small sparks— scintillations that are portions of fire— issue forth, emerging variously and in manifold ways;
and just as these two examples demonstrate activity even in the absence of a difference in the agent,
while prior to such activity there is unity by nature.
In the same way, the meaning is: from this very self consisting of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*), prior to awakening—that which is its true nature—from that [self];
all the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), such as speech and the rest; and all the worlds, such as the earth and the rest.
All fruits of action,
all the gods such as Agni and others who preside over the world of living beings,
and all created beings from Brahmā down to a blade of grass— all classes of living creatures.
In this reading, "all these are selves" means that they are individual selves whose specific characteristics are being awakened through contact with limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*);
they "issue forth.
From which Self this entire world of moving and non-moving beings issues forth incessantly, like sparks from a fire.
And that very Brahman-Ātman, in which [the world] dissolves like a water bubble, and of whose nature it consists during the period of its existence— of that Ātman, this [is the teaching].

*Upaniṣad*: that word which brings [one] near (*upa*) and leads [one] to the goal (*nigamayati*) is called *upaniṣad*. Based on the authority of the scripture, this specific quality inherent in the word is determined, namely its nature as a "bringer-near. To the question "What is this *upaniṣad*? he says: "The Truth of Truth."
For this Upaniṣad is indeed difficult to understand in its meaning everywhere, because its subject matter is non-worldly;
thus, he explains its meaning: "The vital breaths (prāṇas) are indeed truth, and he is the truth of them.
Two subsequent Brāhmaṇas will serve as the explanation of this very sentence.
Let it be that the two subsequent Brāhmaṇas are for the purpose of explaining the Upaniṣad;

it has been stated, "Its Upaniṣad," but regarding this we do not know: does this Upaniṣad belong to the transmigrating self consisting of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*), who was previously mentioned, who rose by the pressing of the hands, and who experiences sound and other objects, or rather to some other non-transmigrating self?
What follows from this?
If it is a transmigrating being, then that very transmigrating being is what must be known; through the knowledge of that alone, all is attained.
That very [Self] is what is denoted by the word "Brahman," and the knowledge of that alone is "brahmavidyā.
Alternatively, if [Brahman] refers to the non-transmigrating [Self],
then the knowledge having that as its object is brahmavidyā.
And from that realization of Brahman, there would be the attainment of all states of being;
all this will come to pass through the authority of the scriptures.

However, in this view, the scriptural passages that establish the identity with the Supreme Brahman—such as "One should meditate [on the Self] as the Self alone" and "I have known the Self alone as 'I am Brahman'"—would be contradicted.
Furthermore, since there would be no transmigrating soul other than [Brahman], instruction would be purposeless.
Precisely because this is a ground for great delusion even for the learned— a subject regarding which questions remain unanswered despite replies— therefore,
we shall investigate the statements that set forth the knowledge of Brahman to the best of our ability, for the sake of developing the intellect of those who desire to know Brahman.

First of all, the Supreme is not one who does not transmigrate, because scripture declares His birth from the one who is awakened by the pressing of hands and who experiences sound and other objects, being distinguished by a different state.
Nor is there a Supreme who is free from hunger and so forth and is merely a ruler; why is that?

For, having made the promise, "I shall make Brahman known," the Śruti awakens the sleeping person by a touch of the hand, leads him through the door of dreaming to another state called deep sleep, and from that very Self characterized by the state of deep sleep, demonstrates its origin by means of the analogies of sparks from a fire and the spider, with the words beginning, "In this very way, from this [Self]... and so forth.
Nor is any other cause of the origin of the world heard of in the intervening context;
for this is indeed the section concerning that which consists of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*).
And in another scriptural passage within the same section, the Kauṣītakins, having introduced the persons within the sun and so forth, state: "He said: 'Who..."

"O Bālāka, he who is the maker of these persons, or whose work this is— he indeed is to be known"; thus [the text] shows that it is the one consisting of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*) who has awakened that is to be known, not any other entity.

And likewise, having stated, "But for the sake of the Self, everything becomes dear," [the text] shows that it is precisely this well-known dear Self which is to be seen, heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon. Furthermore,

at the time of introducing knowledge, there would be consistency with such statements as "One should meditate [upon the Self] as the Self alone," "This is dearer than a son, dearer than wealth," and "He knew only the Self as 'I am Brahman,'" provided that anything else superior [to the Self] does not exist.
And it will be said: "If a person were to know himself as 'I am this'...
Furthermore, in all the Vedāntas, it is shown that Brahman is to be known only as the inner self through the notion of "I," and not as something external to be known like sound and other objects.

Likewise, in the Kauṣītaki [Upaniṣad] itself, by the passage beginning, “One should not seek to know speech; one should know the speaker,” it shows that the agent alone, distinguished from the instruments such as speech and so forth, is the object to be known. If it be argued that he is a non-transmigrating being characterized by a different state—namely, that the one consisting of consciousness who experiences sound and other objects in the waking state is indeed the same one who, having entered another state called deep sleep, becomes a non-transmigrating being, the supreme ruler, and something else—that is not so.
Because it has not been observed;
for no such entity possessing these characteristics has ever been observed, except according to the tenets of the Nihilists (Vaināśikas).
Indeed, in the world, a cow remains a cow whether it is standing or walking.
"Even when lying down, it remains a different genus such as 'horse' and so forth.
And this follows from logic: whatever property a category of object is known to possess through valid cognition, it possesses that very same property even in other places, times, and states.
If that nature were to deviate [from its definition], all conventional discourse based on valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) would be subverted;
accordingly, the experts in logic, such as the Sāṅkhyas and Mīmāṃsakas, demonstrate through hundreds of arguments the non-existence of one who is not subject to saṃsāra.

If it is argued that [the transmigrating soul] is unfit [to be the creator], because even for a transmigrating being there is an absence of the knowledge of being the agent of the acts of the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the world— then that which has been established by you with such great elaboration,
namely, that "it is the transmigrating soul itself, as characterized by a different state, who is here the creator of the world"— that is incorrect;

for the absence of the means and the power of knowledge regarding the agency of the acts of the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the world is directly perceived by everyone in the case of the transmigrating soul.

If it is argued that this is unreasonable—asking how a transmigrating being such as ourselves could create the world, characterized by the specific arrangement of the earth and other elements, which is impossible even for the mind to conceive—the answer is no, because of scripture. Scripture shows the origin of the world and so forth from a transmigrating being, stating: "In this very way, from this Self... and so on.
Therefore, the position may be that everything is to be accepted on faith:
