"He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving"; "He who transcends hunger and thirst"; "Unattached, for he does not cling"; "By the command of this Imperishable"; "He who, dwelling within all beings, is the inner controller, the immortal"; "He who, having led those persons out, passed beyond them."

This is known from hundreds of scriptural passages, such as: “Verily, this great unborn Self”; “He is the bridge, the sustainer”; “The controller of all, the lord of all”; “That Self which is free from evil, ageless, and deathless”; “He created that light”; “In the beginning, this was indeed the Self alone”; and “He is untouched by the suffering of the world, being external to it.”
And from the Smṛti—namely, "I am the source of all; from me everything proceeds"—it follows that there exists a Supreme Being who is beyond transmigratory existence.
This is established by Śruti, Smṛti, and reasoning.
And He is the cause of the universe.
It has been argued that the phrase "from this very Self" shows the origin of the transmigrating soul itself; but this is not so.
Since the Supreme Self is the subject under discussion in the passage, “This space within the heart,” it is appropriate that the reference “from this Self” refers to the Supreme alone.
As an answer to the question, “Where was he then? the Supreme Self, denoted by the word “space,” is stated as: “He lies in that space which is within the heart. [This is further supported by:
“Then, my dear, he becomes united with Being,” and “Day after day they go to this world of Brahman, yet they do not find it.”
From such scriptural passages as “embraced by the wise Self” and “he is firmly established in the supreme Self,” it is determined that the word *ākāśa* refers to the supreme Self;
furthermore, this is confirmed because the word *ātman* is applied to that very same entity after introducing it with the words, “In this, there is a small *ākāśa*.”
The Supreme Self alone is the primordial cause;

therefore, it is entirely logical that the creation proceeds from this Self—that is, from the Supreme Self alone. Furthermore, we have already stated that the transmigrating soul lacks the capacity for the knowledge required for the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the world.

And here, the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) has been introduced with the words, "One should meditate [on it] as the Self alone" and "I have known the Self alone: I am Brahman. Furthermore, the realization of Brahman has its object in Brahman;
thus, it was commenced with the words, "I shall tell you of Brahman" and "I shall cause you to know Brahman."

In this regard, one might object: "Now, Brahman is non-transmigratory, the cause of the world, beyond hunger and other such needs, and by nature eternally pure, conscious, and free; whereas the transmigrating self is the opposite of that. Therefore, one should not grasp 'I am Brahman. For how could one who is base, by recollecting the supreme Lord as the transmigrating self, not become a partaker of fault? Thus, it is more appropriate [to think] 'I am not Brahman'."

Therefore, one should seek to propitiate [Brahman] through offerings of flowers, water, handfuls of water, hymns of praise, prostrations, oblations, gifts, recitation of sacred texts, meditation, yoga, and so forth.
Having known the Lord of All through such propitiation, one becomes Brahman;
one should not, however, contemplate the non-transmigrating Brahman as having the nature of a transmigrating self, just as one would not contemplate fire as cold or space as possessing form.
Even the scripture that establishes the identity of Brahman with the Self would become a mere *arthavāda* (explanatory or commendatory statement),
and thus there would be no contradiction with any system of logic or worldly reasoning.
This is not so, because from the declarations of the Mantras and Brāhmaṇas, the entry of that very [Self] is heard.

Having introduced the subject with “In the beginning [He] created the wheels,” the texts show—in thousands of mantra-statements across all Vedic branches—that it is the non-transmigrating creator alone who enters the body, as in: “The Person entered into the bodies”; “He became the counterpart of every form; that was His form for the purpose of perception”; and “The Wise One, having fashioned all forms and created names, abides calling them forth.”
Likewise, there are the declarations of the Brāhmaṇas:
"Having created that, he entered into it"; "He, having split open this very aperture, entered by this door";
"This deity, having entered these three deities by means of this living self (jīva-ātman)"; "This Self is hidden in all beings."
[The texts] beginning with "It does not shine" [are thus explained].

Furthermore, because the word *ātman* is employed for Brahman in all the Vedas, and because the word *ātman* denotes the inner self (*pratyagātman*), and because of the Vedic scripture stating "He is the inner Self of all beings," there is no transmigrating soul apart from the Supreme Self; [this is established by the text] "One only, without a second."

From such scriptural passages as "Brahman alone is this" and "The Self alone is this," it is indeed proper to ascertain that "I am Brahman. When the meaning of the scripture stands thus, then the Supreme Self would possess the state of being a transmigrator; and that being the case, the futility of the scripture results. Alternatively, if He were not a transmigrator, the futility of the instruction would follow; thus a clear defect is incurred.

If, first of all, the Supreme Self—the inner self of all beings—were to experience the sufferings produced by contact with all bodies, then the transmigratory state (*saṃsāritva*) of the Supreme would clearly result;
and thus the Śruti texts and Smṛtis that establish the non-transmigratory nature of the Supreme, as well as all logical arguments (*nyāya*), would be contradicted.

Alternatively, if it could somehow be established that the Supreme Self is not connected with the sufferings born of association with the bodies of living beings, then the fault of the futility of instruction (*upadeśānarthakya*) would follow, because there would be nothing for the Supreme to achieve or avoid.
It cannot be prevented.
On this point, some offer the following rebuttal:
the Supreme Self has not entered into beings directly in its own form.
Rather, having entered into a state of modification, it attained the nature of the self of consciousness (*vijñānātman*).
And that self of consciousness is both different from and non-different from the Supreme.
Insofar as it is different, it is connected with transmigratory existence (*saṃsāritva*); insofar as it is non-different, it is fit to be determined as "I am Brahman."
In this way, everything will be consistent.

In that regard, regarding the position that the conscious self (*vijñānātman*) is a modification [of the Supreme Self], these are the possible courses: either the conscious self is a partial transformation of the Supreme Self—which, like the substance of the earth, is composed of an aggregate of many substances and possesses parts—just as a jar or similar object [is a transformation]; or else, a portion of the Supreme Self, while remaining in its prior state of configuration, undergoes modification, just as hair, salt-encrusted ground, and so forth [are modifications].

Or rather, the entire other [entity] might transform, like milk and so forth. In that case, when some particular substance within a collection of many substances of the same genus attains the nature of consciousness,
then because of their common genus, their oneness is merely figurative and not in the ultimate sense.

And this being the case, there would be a contradiction with the established doctrine (*siddhānta*). Now, if the supreme Self (*para ātmā*) is the whole (*avayavī*) which follows its eternal and inseparably established parts (*nityāyutasiddhāvayava*),

and if the transmigrating conscious self (*vijñānātman*) is but one part of that [Self] while it remains in that state— then, because the whole pervades all its parts, any defect or quality residing in a part must belong to the whole itself.

The notion that the supreme Self itself becomes connected with the defect of transmigratory existence due to the nature of the individual consciousness (vijñānātman) is also an undesirable hypothesis; furthermore,
if one maintains the position that everything undergoes transformation like milk, there would be a contradiction with all the Śruti and Smṛti scriptures.
And that [position] is undesirable, because [the Self is described as]:

"partless, actionless, and tranquil"; "for the divine Person is formless, existing both within and without, and unborn"; "all-pervading and eternal like space"; "this indeed is the great unborn Self, undecaying, immortal, and deathless"; and "it is never born, nor does it ever die."
All these positions are contradicted by Śruti, Smṛti, and reasoning, beginning with the statement, "This [Self] is unmanifest.

Regarding the position that the individual self (vijñānātman) is a part of the immovable Supreme Self, it has been stated that the transmigratory wandering through various locations—characteristic of one who experiences the fruits of karma—is impossible; or else, the Supreme Self itself would be subject to transmigration.

If it is argued that a portion of the Supreme, like a spark from a fire, breaks off as the conscious self (*vijñānātman*) and transmigrates— even so, by the breaking off of a limb of the Supreme, injury would be incurred; and upon its transmigration, there would result a vacuity due to the shifting of parts to another region of the Supreme Self,
which contradicts scriptural statements regarding His being without wound (*avraṇatva*).

If it is argued that there is no fault because the scriptural texts on fire-sparks and other such examples show that when the conscious self— which constitutes a limb of the Supreme Self— transmigrates, the Supreme Self does not incur suffering (as if from a heart-piercing pain) due to the displacement and expansion of another part, since there is no empty space devoid of the Supreme Self;
we say no, because scripture serves only as an indicator [of what is already established by reason].
The scripture is not intended to alter the nature of things;
what then? It is for the purpose of making known those things as they truly are, which have not been previously known.
What follows from this? Listen—therefore, that which occurs [is as follows]:
Just as the properties of entities such as the formed (*mūrta*) and the formless (*amūrta*) are well-known in the world as they truly are,

the scripture proceeds to make known another reality that is not in contradiction with them by employing those very examples; it does not employ a worldly example for the purpose of making known something that contradicts worldly reality.
Even if an example were adduced, it would be useless because it would not correspond to the subject of the illustration;
for it is impossible to establish— even with a hundred examples— that fire is cold or that the sun does not burn,
since the nature of the thing has been otherwise apprehended by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Furthermore, one means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is not contradicted by another means of valid cognition,
for one means of valid cognition makes known only that which is not the object of another means of valid cognition.
Moreover, it is not possible for scripture (āgama) to cause the understanding of some other unknown reality apart from its reliance on worldly words and word-meanings.

Therefore, for one who follows established logic, it is impossible to demonstrate that the Supreme Self possesses parts or is composed of parts and portions from the perspective of ultimate reality. If it is argued that this is so because it is heard in the Śruti and remembered in the Smṛti— namely, “the tiny sparks” and “a portion of My very self”—
we say no, because those passages have the purpose of establishing the realization of oneness.
For in the world, a spark of fire is seen to be fit for the cognition of identity with fire itself;
likewise, a part is fit for the cognition of identity with the whole.

This being so, those words which express that the individual self (vijñānātman) is a modification or a part of the supreme self (paramātman) intend to bring about the cognition of its identity with the supreme self.
And from both the opening and the conclusion: for in all the Upaniṣads, having first proposed non-duality,
and having established that the world is a modification or a part of the Supreme Self through illustrations and reasons, they finally conclude once again with non-duality.

For instance, right here [in this very text], having first made the proposition, "All this is what this Self is," and having established the grounds for the cognition of oneness—such as the fact that the cause and effect are not different—by means of examples regarding the causes of origin, subsistence, and dissolution, [the author] will conclude with, "Without interior or exterior; this Self is Brahman.
Therefore, he will bring together the beginning and the conclusion.

Therefore, by means of the opening and the conclusion, this meaning is determined: that the passages teaching origination, subsistence, and dissolution serve to strengthen the realization of the oneness of the Supreme Self.

Furthermore, otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence of a split in the sentence (*vākya-bheda*); for there is no disagreement among all proponents of the Upaniṣads that in all the Upaniṣads the realization of the oneness of the individual self (*vijñānātman*) and the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) is enjoined.
And since it is possible for the passages concerning origination and so forth to form a single syntactical unit with that injunction, there is no evidence [for their independent authority].

Furthermore, one would have to postulate another result [for the knowledge of the Self]; therefore, the scriptural texts concerning origination and so forth are intended solely to establish the oneness of the Self.

In this regard, those who know the tradition relate the following narrative: it is said that a certain son of a king was abandoned by his parents immediately after birth and reared in the house of a hunter.
Not knowing his true lineage, he follows only the actions of the hunter caste due to his conviction that he belongs to that species;
he does not follow the actions of the royal caste with the thought, "I am a king.

However, when someone of supreme compassion, recognizing the prince's fitness for attaining royal glory, awakens him to his sonship, saying: "You are not a hunter; you are the son of such-and-such a king," [he then realizes his true nature].

"Having somehow entered the house of a hunter"— thus enlightened, he abandons the karmas conditioned by his birth as a hunter and follows his own ancestral path of his father and grandfathers, thinking, "I am a king. Likewise, this [Self], though originally non-transmigratory, having become differentiated from the Supreme like a spark of fire and the like, enters here into the thicket of the body, senses, and so forth,
and follows the transmigratory attributes of the body and senses, thinking, "I am this aggregate of body and senses."
One who does not know the true nature of the Self thinks, "I am thin," "I am fat," "I am happy," or "I am miserable.

However, when enlightened by the teacher that "you are not of this nature; you are indeed the Supreme Brahman, free from saṃsāra," he abandons the pursuit of the three desires and realizes, "I am Brahman.

In this regard, the realization of Brahman becomes firm, just as a prince's realization of his own royalty becomes firm. This is because, when told, "You have fallen from the Supreme Brahman like a spark," one perceives the identity of the spark with fire even before its fall from the fire, just as a spark is seen to be one with the fire prior to its separation.

Therefore, the analogies of gold, a gem, iron, fire, and sparks are intended to strengthen the conviction of oneness (*ekatva*), and are not aimed at establishing distinctions such as origination and so forth;

for it is determined that there is a continuous single flavor (*ekarasa*) in designation (*prajñapti*), like a lump of salt, and because of the scriptural statement: "It should be viewed as one alone."
Furthermore, if the manifold variety of attributes such as origination and so forth— like a painted cloth or like trees and oceans— were intended to be made known regarding Brahman,

[the scripture] would not have concluded with "without interior or exterior, like a mass of salt, of one essence," nor would it have employed the instruction, "It is to be viewed as one alone," nor the deprecatory statement, "He who sees here as if there were multiplicity."

Therefore, the conceptualization of [the world's] origin, maintenance, dissolution, and so forth in all the Vedāntas is solely for the sake of strengthening the conviction that the one [Brahman] is of a single nature,
not for the purpose of producing a cognition of that [world].
Nor is it reasonable to postulate a transmigrating part within the partless Supreme Self, which is itself non-transmigrating.
Because the Supreme Self is by its very nature without location (*adeśatva*),

if one were to imagine that the Supreme, which is without location, possesses transmigration in only one part, it would follow that the Supreme itself is imagined to be the transmigrating being. Alternatively, if it is argued that a single part of the Supreme is produced by an external limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), [the same fault remains].
It is like the space within a jar or a water-pot;
at that time, the notion does not arise in the discerning that "a portion of the Supreme Self here is a part of a separate conventional usage.
If it is argued that such a figurative notion is observed both among the non-discerning and the discerning?
No; because for those lacking discrimination it is a false cognition,

and for those possessing discrimination it serves merely as a basis for conventional usage— just as when the sky is said to be "black" or "red," even for those possessing discrimination, its blackness or redness is understood to serve merely as a basis for conventional usage.
In the ultimate sense, space cannot be black or red; therefore,

wise men should not entertain notions regarding the realization of the nature of Brahman such as part and whole, portion and that which possesses the portion, or modification and that which is modified, because all the Upaniṣads have as their sole purport the removal of all conceptual constructions and the attainment of the essential reality.

Therefore, having abandoned all conceptualization, one should realize the state of being without distinction, like space, on the basis of hundreds of scriptural passages such as: "All-pervading and eternal like space," and "It is not tainted by the suffering of the world, being external.

One should not conceive of the Self as distinct from Brahman, just as one would not conceive of a cold spot in fire, whose nature is heat, or a dark spot in the sun, whose nature is light; for the purpose of all the Upaniṣads is to culminate in the removal of all conceptualization.

Therefore, all worldly transactions regarding the Self—which is by nature free from the attributes of transmigratory existence—are caused solely by the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) of name-and-form (nāmarūpa).
This is evident from such Vedic mantras as: "He assumed form after form," and "The Wise One, having fashioned all forms and created names, abides calling them forth.
Transmigratory existence does not belong to the Self by its own nature.
It is merely an illusion, like the cognition of a red crystal produced by contact with an adjunct such as lac-dye, and not so in ultimate reality. [As it is said:
"He meditates, as it were; He moves, as it were"; "He does not increase by action, nor does He become smaller"; "He is not smeared by evil action."
Based on such scriptural and traditional authorities as, “Abiding equally in all beings,” and “In the dog and even in the outcaste,” and according to logical reasoning,
the Supreme Self is indeed non-transmigrating.

Therefore, when its partless nature is accepted, it is impossible to specifically entertain the alternatives that the individual soul (vijñānātman) is either a partial portion, a modification, a power, or something else entirely.

We have already stated that the scriptural and traditional declarations concerning portions (*aṃśa*) and so forth have the purpose of establishing oneness, and do not aim to demonstrate difference, because they form a single syntactical unit (*ekavākya*) whose intended meaning is unity.

If all the Upaniṣads are devoted solely to making known the unity of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), then for what purpose is a contrary meaning—the distinction of the individual self (*vijñānātman*)—imagined? Some say it is to avoid contradicting the authority of the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*). For the sentences that enjoin rituals are based upon various actions, instruments, results, enjoyers, and agents;

if there were no distinction of the individual self, and if the Supreme Self alone were non-transmigrating and one, how could those [sentences] induce one to engage in rituals that have desirable fruits?
Or would they cause [beings] to turn away from actions that have undesirable results?
For whose liberation, moreover, would the Upaniṣads be undertaken?
Furthermore, in the view that asserts the oneness of the supreme self, how could there be an instruction regarding the oneness of the supreme self?
Or what is the fruit of receiving that instruction?
For instruction is intended for one who is bound, in order to destroy their bondage; in the absence of such a person, the Upaniṣadic scripture would indeed be without a subject.

If this is so, then the path of objection and resolution regarding the position of the proponents of the Upaniṣads is identical to that of the proponents of the ritual section (karmakāṇḍa)—by which, in the absence of difference [between the self and the agent], the ritual section, being without a foundation, cannot establish itself.
The Upaniṣads are likewise [authoritative] with respect to their own validity.
If that is so, then let the authority belong only to that section on ritual action (*karmakāṇḍa*), for which there is no contradiction of its own meaning in its validity.
However, if one were to assume the authority of the Upaniṣads, it would result in the subversion of their own literal meaning; thus, let there be no such authority.
For the ritual section (karmakāṇḍa), being authoritative, cannot become non-authoritative;
indeed, a lamp does not fail to illuminate that which is to be illuminated.

And it does not reveal [it]. Furthermore, because it contradicts means of valid cognition such as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), the Upaniṣads— not only subvert their own purpose by establishing the oneness of Brahman, but also subvert the authority of the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*)—
are moreover in conflict with those means of valid cognition whose objects are the distinctions determined by direct perception and other such means.
Therefore, the Upaniṣads are either devoid of authority,
or they may have some other purpose;
but they certainly do not have the purpose of establishing the oneness of Brahman.
No; for the answer has already been stated.

For the validity or invalidity of a means of knowledge (pramāṇa) is based on its producing or not producing a valid cognition (pramā); otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that pillars and the like would possess the status of being means of knowledge with respect to objects of knowledge such as sound.
What follows from this? If the Upaniṣads indeed produce the valid cognition of the oneness of Brahman, how could they be non-authoritative?

You who speak thus must be asked: does your statement intended to negate the authority of the Upaniṣads not itself effect the negation of that authority, just as fire effects the manifestation of form?
Now, suppose he acts;
if he acts, then let your statement, which is a means of valid cognition for the purpose of negation, be so,
and let fire be the illuminator of form.
If the authority of prohibitive statements is established, then the authority of the Upaniṣads is indeed established.
On this point, let your honors state: what is the resolution?

Is it not the case that here, in the sentence "Do not touch fire," there is the valid cognition (*pramā*) consisting of the comprehension of the meaning of the prohibition of the authority of the Upaniṣads, and in the case of fire, the valid cognition consisting of the comprehension of its form and its capacity to illuminate?

What, then, is your hostility toward the Upaniṣads, which are found to provide direct perception as a means of valid knowledge regarding the realization of the oneness of Brahman? For a prohibition [of their authority] is untenable.
Furthermore, we have already stated that the cessation of sorrow, delusion, and so forth is the perceptible fruit produced through the successive stages of the realization of the oneness of Brahman.
Therefore, since this has already been answered, there is no room for any suspicion regarding the lack of validity of the Upaniṣads.
As for what was stated— that it lacks authority because it subverts its own meaning—
that too is not correct, because there is no sublation of the comprehension of that meaning.
For there is no understanding derived from the Upaniṣads that "Brahman alone is one without a second" and "not even this."

Just as from the sentence "fire is hot and cold" there arises the comprehension of two contradictory meanings, we have spoken thus having provisionally accepted this point; however, according to the established rule regarding the authority of speech, it is not the case that a single sentence can have multiple meanings.
And if there were multiple meanings, there would be the primary meaning,
and another contradictory meaning that would obstruct it.
However, for those who take this very sentence as their authority, there is no contradiction between what is opposed and what is not opposed;
such is the established principle that a single sentence can convey multiple meanings.
Because there is unity of purpose, there is unity of sentence.
Furthermore, no Upaniṣadic passages negate the oneness of Brahman.
As for the worldly statement, "Fire is hot and cold," [it is not intended as a single unitary proposition].
There is no syntactic unity there,
because one part of it merely restates an object already known through another means of valid cognition;
for example, "Fire is cold" constitutes a single sentence.
The statement "fire is hot," however, merely serves to recall an experience gained through another means of valid cognition;
it does not itself bring about the comprehension of the object.
Therefore, it cannot form a single syntactical unit with the statement "fire is not cold."
This is because [the sentence] is exhausted merely by reminding one of an experience through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

As for the thought that this sentence expresses a contradictory meaning, that is an error caused by the application of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word "fire" alongside the words "cold" and "hot."
However, neither a worldly nor a Vedic sentence can have multiple meanings.
As for the claim that an Upaniṣadic statement subverts the authority of the Karma-kāṇḍa,
that is not so, because it has a different purpose.

For the Upaniṣads, being intent upon establishing the oneness of Brahman, do not preclude the instruction of means for attaining a desired goal, nor do they forbid the application of human effort toward that end; this is precisely because it is impossible for them to have more than one primary purpose.
Furthermore, it is not the case that valid knowledge regarding their own respective meanings fails to arise from the sentences of the ritual section (Karmakāṇḍa).
If a sentence produces valid cognition regarding its own unique object, how could there be a contradiction with anything else?
If it is argued that, because the oneness of Brahman is devoid of objective content, no valid cognition arises at all—then [we reply]: no.
No, because valid cognition is perceptible.
From such sentences as "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa" and "A Brāhmaṇa must not be killed," a perceptible valid cognition arises;
that [cognition] would certainly not fail to exist.
If it is argued that there is an inference— namely, "the Upanishads will bring about the knowledge of the oneness of Brahman"—
inference does not attain validity when it contradicts direct perception. Therefore, this which is being asserted— that valid cognition simply does not arise— is indeed false.

Moreover, by relying on the very agency, action, and result as they are conventionally perceived and presented by ignorance, the Śruti— addressing one who is engaged in the general means for attaining the desired and avoiding the undesired, yet does not know their specific details— neither declares the truth nor denies the falsity of the distinctions between action, agent, and result that are well-known in the world.
This is because [the scripture] is devoted to prescribing the means for attaining desired fruits and avoiding undesired ones.

For example, the Vedic revelation (*śruti*) engaged in rites for specific desires (*kāmya-karma*), even though desires arise from false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*), accepts desires exactly as they are found and prescribes only their means;
it does not, however, prescribe that desires are of the nature of misfortune simply because they arise from false knowledge.

Likewise, the scripture concerning the obligatory *agnihotra* and other rites also prescribes such actions as the *agnihotra* and so forth, perceiving some purpose— either the attainment of a specific desired end or the avoidance of a specific undesired one— by taking for granted the distinctions between action and agent as they appear, which arise from false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*). It does not fail to operate, as it does with optional rites (*kāmya*), by having as its object unreal things that fall within the domain of ignorance (*avidyā*).
Nor would persons lacking knowledge fail to engage in activity,
because it is observed that those possessed of desire do so.
If it is argued that only those possessing knowledge have the qualification for ritual action?
No, for it has already been stated that there is a contradiction with the qualification for ritual action (*karma*) within the knowledge of the oneness of Brahman.

By this, it should be understood that the refutation of the fault regarding the lack of a result from grasping [the truth] through instruction—on the grounds that [Brahman] is without an object when its oneness is realized—is also explained.
Furthermore, due to the diversity of human desires, such as passion and so forth, the desires of persons are indeed manifold.
Furthermore, defects such as passion and the like are manifold;
therefore, the scripture is not able to turn back one whose mind has been carried away by passion for external objects,
nor is it able to incite one who is by nature detached from external objects toward those same objects.

However, from scripture there occurs only this much: the manifestation of the specific relationship between the goal and the means, namely, "this is a means to the desired" and "this is a means to the undesired"—just as a lamp [reveals] the knowledge of forms and so forth in the dark.
Scripture does not, like a servant, forcibly turn one away or compel one to act;
for indeed, people are seen transgressing even scripture due to the weight of passion and other such impulses.
Therefore, with regard to the diversity of human intellects, [the Teacher] teaches the various specific relationships between means and ends in many ways.
In this regard, individuals engage themselves according to their own preference among the specific means;
the scripture, however, remains indifferent, like the sun or a lamp.
Likewise, for someone else, even that which is not a human goal (apuruṣārtha) may appear as if it were a human goal (puruṣārtha);
whatever appearance something has for a person, that person perceives the human goal to be of that very form.
One seeks the means of accomplishment that correspond to those [ends].
Likewise, there is also an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*): “Three sons of Prajāpati lived the life of a religious student (*brahmacarya*) with their father Prajāpati,” and so forth.
Therefore, the Vedāntas, intending to make known the oneness of Brahman, do not sublate the scripture of injunctions.
Nor does the injunctional scripture become devoid of subject matter by this much;
nor does the injunctional scripture, with its aforementioned distinctions of factors of action (*kāraka*) and so forth, subvert the authority of the Upaniṣads regarding the oneness of Brahman.
For means of knowledge are indeed "heroic" within their own respective domains.
Like the sense of hearing and so forth.
In this regard, some who consider themselves wise, by the power of their own minds, regard all means of valid cognition as mutually contradictory;

they even raise objections regarding the contradiction with perception and other means of knowledge concerning the oneness of Brahman, saying: "Indeed, sound and the other objects of the senses are perceived through direct perception as being distinct from one another."
For those who assert the oneness of Brahman, there would be a contradiction with direct perception;
likewise, through the ears and other senses, perceivers of sound and so forth, as well as agents of merit and demerit, are inferred to be distinct in every body— these being the transmigrating souls—
and thus for those asserting the oneness of Brahman, there is also a contradiction with inference.

Furthermore, they allege a contradiction with scripture based on such statements as, "One desiring a village should sacrifice," "One desiring cattle should sacrifice," and "One desiring heaven should sacrifice. From these sentences, it is understood that those who desire villages, cattle, heaven, and so forth, and those who perform the means for attaining them, are distinct [from the Self].

To this it is replied: those people, whose inner organs are corrupted by fallacious reasoning, are outcasts among the castes such as Brāhmaṇas; they are to be pitied, for their intellects have lost the traditional transmission regarding the meaning of the scriptures.

How so? Those who claim that the oneness of Brahman is contradicted by sound and other objects perceived through direct perception via the doors of the ears and other senses must be asked: "Is the oneness of space contradicted by the diversity of sound and the rest?
Or is it not contradicted?
In that case, there is no contradiction with perception.

As for what was said—that distinct perceivers of sound and so forth, as well as agents of merit and demerit, are inferred for each body, and thus, if Brahman were one, there would be a contradiction with inference; [that argument is refuted].
They should be asked, "By whom are these [differences] inferred?

If they should reply, "By all of us who are skilled in inference," then when they are thus asked, "Who are you who are skilled in inference? what will be their answer? For, upon each of them individually denying skill in inference regarding the body, the sense organs, the mind, and the self, [there would be no response].
If it is argued that "we selves, whose instruments are the body, senses, and mind, are skilled in inference because actions are accomplished by multiple causal factors," then,
in that case, there follows the undesirable consequence of your being many selves due to your skill in inference.
For you yourselves have accepted that an action (*kriyā*) is indeed accomplished by multiple causal factors (*kāraka*).
In this regard, inference is an action;
it has been asserted that it is brought to completion by the causal factors consisting of the body, the senses, the mind, and the self, and that its agent is the self.
In this regard, by those who say, "We are skilled in inference," it would follow that they accept that there are multiple selves, each possessing a body, sense organs, and a mind as its instruments.
Oh, what a display of inferential skill has been shown by these bull-like logicians who lack even tails and horns!
For how could one who does not know the self itself—being so deluded—possibly know anything pertaining to it?
In that case, what does one infer, or by what mark (liṅga)?
For there is no mark whatsoever that establishes the difference of the self per se.
By whatever mark one might seek to establish a difference in the Self;

those marks which they put forward as having name and form in order to prove a difference in the Self are merely adventitious adjuncts (*upādhi*) belonging to name and form, just as jars, water-pots, rooms, and cavities in the earth are to space.
When one perceives a mark of difference in space,
then one would also find a mark of difference in the Self;
for even by hundreds of logicians who admit distinctions in the Self based on something other than itself, it is impossible to demonstrate a mark of difference in the Self.
From its own side, however, it is already removed from afar, because the self is not an object [of cognition].
Whatever the opponent accepts as a property of the self—

Because it is admitted that each [individual] is distinct from the Self by virtue of name and form, according to the Śruti: "Space, indeed, is the bringer-forth of name and form; that which is between them is Brahman," and also, "I shall manifest name and form.
For name and form consist of origination and dissolution.
And Brahman is distinct from that; therefore, since it is not an object of inference at all, how could there be a contradiction with inference?
By this, contradiction with scripture is also refuted. As for what was said regarding the teaching given to someone [else] when Brahman is one:
And as for the argument that the purpose of receiving instruction would be absent [for one who already knows], and therefore the instruction on unity would be useless—
that too is not correct.
Since actions are accomplished by multiple factors, a certain objection arises:
in the case of Brahman, which is one and devoid of limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhika*), there can be neither a teacher nor a teaching.
Nor is there any fruit in receiving instruction;
therefore, the point that the Upaniṣads are purposeless is already accepted.
If it is objected that they are purposeless because they concern multiple causal factors, we say no, not inherently.

Because it contradicts the tenets of those who maintain the existence of a self, this fortress of fearlessness—unassailable by the king-like soldiers of sophistry, inaccessible to those of small intellect, and unreachable by those devoid of the grace of the scriptures and the Guru—is [the domain of the Lord].

This is so because of scriptural and traditional declarations that He is attainable only through His supreme grace, such as: "Who other than Me is able to know that God, who is beyond intoxication and yet the source of intoxication?"; "Even the gods have had doubts regarding this in the past"; and "This wisdom is not to be attained through logic."
This is also evident from the Vedic mantras that reveal the coexistence of contradictory attributes, such as: “It moves; it moves not; it is far; it is near.
And in the *Gītā*: “All beings abide in Me,” and so forth.
Therefore, there is no other distinct entity called a "transmigrating soul" (saṃsārī) apart from the Supreme Brahman.

Therefore, it is rightly said: "In the beginning, this was indeed Brahman; it knew only itself as 'I am Brahman'"; and from hundreds of such scriptural passages as, "There is no other seer than this, there is no other hearer than this. Therefore, the Upanishad whose name is "the Truth of Truth" is the supreme [teaching] concerning the Supreme Brahman alone. 20.
Thus ends the first section, the Brāhmaṇa of Ajātaśatru, in the second chapter of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad Bhāṣya.
START Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.2.1:
"I shall make known Brahman"—thus it was introduced;
therein, it was made known that Brahman is that one [reality] from which the world is born, of which it consists, and into which it dissolves.
Furthermore, of what nature is that world which is born and dissolved?
It is of the nature of the five elements;
and the elements are of the nature of name and form.
It has been stated that name-and-form (nāmarūpa) is the truth;
of that truth, which consists of the five elements, Brahman is the truth. But how are the elements the truth? This is explained in the Mūrtāmūrta Brāhmaṇa.
Since they consist of the elements in both their formed and formless states, the elements and the vital breaths (prāṇas) are indeed real.
With the desire to determine the reality of those elements which consist of effects and instruments, these two Brāhmaṇas are commenced; this is the very explanation of the Upaniṣad.
For, by means of determining the reality of the effects and instruments, Brahman—the "Real of the Real"—is determined.
Regarding this, it has been said: "The vital breaths (prāṇas) are indeed truth; of them, this [Self] is the truth.
In that regard, what are the vital breaths?
How many Upaniṣads concerning the vital breaths are there? And which are they?
And thus, in connection with the *Brahmopaniṣad*, he determines the true nature of the instruments, the vital breaths (*prāṇas*), like one who discerns a well or a garden encountered on a path:
"He who knows the infant together with its support, its receptacle, its pillar, and its tether, verily wards off seven hostile rivals.
This indeed is the infant, which is this middle vital breath."
Of this, this is the support and this is the secondary support; the vital breath is the pillar and food is the rope.
Whoever knows the child together with its support, its counter-support, its pillar, and its rope—for him there is this fruit: what is it?
Seven, that is, seven in number, his hateful rivals who act with malice.
For adversaries are of two kinds:
those who hate and those who do not hate;
among them, he wards off those adversaries who are hateful enemies.
The seven vital breaths located in the head are the gateways for the perception of objects; the attachments to those objects, arising from them, are "enemies" because they are innate.
For these indeed turn one's vision, which resides in one's own self, toward the objects of the senses;
therefore, they are enemies who hate.

Because it functions to prohibit the investigation of the inner self (*pratyagātman*), it is stated in the *Kaṭha Upaniṣad*: “The Self-existent pierced the sense-apertures outward; therefore one looks outward, not at the inner self,” and so forth.
In that context, he who knows the child and the rest—
He determines their true nature;
he thus obstructs these rivals, opens them up, and destroys them.
To him, who has become attentive through the hearing of this result, [the teacher] says: "This, indeed, is the infant."
Who is he? He is this middle vital breath (prāṇa), the vital breath within the body which is the subtle body (liṅgātman),
that which has entered the body in five ways, and which is called "the great one, clad in white garments, King Soma."

In whom the organs, beginning with speech and mind, are fastened— as illustrated by the example of the pegs of a six-sided tethering post— he is like a child, because he lacks proficiency regarding sense objects, just as other organs do.
It has been stated that the "infant" (*śiśu*) is the substratum (*ādhāna*).
But what is the substratum of that infant, which stands in the place of the calf and consists of the instruments (*karaṇa*)?
This very body is its substratum, being of the nature of an effect (*kārya*); it is called a "substratum" (*ādhāna*) because [the infant] is supported (*ādhiyate*) within it.
For this body is the substratum of that vital breath (prāṇa),
for it is upon this [body] that the instruments are established; having attained their own nature, they become gateways for perception,
but they are not attached to the mere vital breath alone.
For it has been shown by Ajātaśatru that when the organs have been withdrawn, that which consists of consciousness (vijñānamaya) is not perceived;

but when the organs are distributed throughout the regions of the body, that which consists of consciousness is perceived as being present. And this was demonstrated by the awakening through the pressing of the hand. This head is the respective receptacle (pratyādhāna).
It is called *pratyādhāna* because it is placed (*ādhīyate*) in various specific locations (*pradeśaviśeṣeṣu*).

Life-force (*prāṇa*) is the pillar; power (*bala*) produced by food and drink is synonymous with life-force (*prāṇa*), for life-force is the support of strength in this body, as seen in the scriptural passage: "When this self, having fallen into weakness, enters as it were into a state of confusion... (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.35).

Just as a calf is supported by a tethering post, some say that the vital air (prāṇa) which clings to the body is the tethering post; food is the rope— for food, when eaten, is transformed into three parts,
of which the gross transformation is [the body].
Having become these two, it approaches this [body]: urine and feces.

That which is the intermediate essence (rasa) accumulates its own effect—the body composed of the seven constituent elements (saptadhātuka)—through the sequence beginning with blood; for the body is nourished by the arrival of food, which is its own source, because the body consists of food.
In the opposite case, it diminishes and falls away; however,
that which is the most excellent essence— called nectar (*amṛta*) and the power of vitality (*ūrj-prabhāva*)—
having reached the region of the heart from above the navel, [remains there].

Having entered into the seventy-two thousand channels that radiate from the heart, that which is the subtle body (*liṅga*)—known as the "child" (*śiśu*) and consisting of an aggregate of instruments—has its cause for stability within the physical body in the form of what is called "the pillar" (*sthūṇā*), which generates strength.
By means of this, food becomes a bond between the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the body, like a calf tied on both sides by a rope. //1//
START BṛhUp 2.2.2:
Now, certain Upaniṣads regarding that very infant who has been carried to his resting place in the eye are being stated:
these seven imperishable ones wait upon him.
Thus, with those red streaks that are on the eye, Rudra is connected to it; with the waters that are in the eye, Parjanya is connected;
and with the pupil, Āditya is connected.
That which is black, by that it is Agni;
that which is white, by that it is Indra.
To this lower track, the earth is attached.
The sky is the upper [lid].
The food of one who knows thus is never exhausted. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.2.2)

These seven imperishables attend upon him—that village consisting of the instruments [of perception], which is bound to food in the body and situated in the eye. Although the root *sthā* preceded by *upa* takes the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) when used with a mantra as its instrument, here too there are seven designations of deities that stand in the place of mantras, serving as the instruments. These seven imperishables attend upon it because they are the causes of its imperishability.
Therefore, even here, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) after the root *sthā* is not contradictory.
What are those "unwinking ones" (*akṣitayaḥ*)?
It is said: they are those well-known [rivers] there.
The "red ones" (*lohinyaḥ*) are the red streaks or lines on the axle;

Rudra is attached to, that is, follows after, this central vital breath (*prāṇa*) by means of those [streaks] which serve as his gateways. Furthermore, there are the waters on the axle which are manifested through contact with smoke and other elements.
By means of those waters, which serve as gateways, Parjanya—the self of the deity—is followed and attends upon [the vital breath]; that is to say, he is present.
And he, having become food, is the imperishable sustenance of the vital breath.
For another scriptural passage states: "When Parjanya rains, the vital breaths become joyful.
Through that pupil—the power of sight—Aditya attends upon the middle vital breath (the breath in the mouth);
and by that which is black in the eye, Agni attends upon it.
That which is white in the eye is Indra;
by the lower eyelid and the lashes, the earth is connected to it,
due to the commonality of being below.
These seven, having become food, wait constantly upon the vital breath (prāṇa). For one who knows this, this is the fruit: his food is never exhausted, provided he knows thus. //2//
Regarding this, there is this verse:
"A ladle with its opening below and its bottom above— in it is placed glory of every form."

"Upon its bank sit the seven seers; speech is the eighth, communicating with Brahman—this is the bowl turned downward with its mouth facing this way and its bottom facing upward. This refers to this very body, for it is indeed a bowl turned downward with its mouth facing this way and its bottom facing upward.
"In him glory is deposited, all-formed"—
glory, indeed, is the vital breaths;
it is the vital breaths that he thus refers to.
"Of that non-existent one, there were seven seers on the bank"—
the seers are indeed the vital breaths;
he says this regarding the vital breaths.
"Speech, as the eighth, comes together with Brahman"—
for speech, as the eighth, indeed comes together with Brahman.

In this regard, concerning this very matter, there is this verse as a mantra, beginning with "The ladle has its opening downward" (arvāgbilaścamasaḥ). Regarding that, the Śruti explains the meaning of the mantra: "The ladle has its opening downward, its bottom upward," and so forth.
But what is this ladle that has its opening downward and its bottom upward?
It is this very head, for it is shaped like a ladle.
How so? For this [space] has its opening toward the front (*arvāgbila*), because the mouth is of the nature of an opening;
it has its bottom turned upward (*ūrdhvabudhna*), because the head is of the shape of a base.
In that [space], "glory of every form" (*yaśo viśvarūpam*) is deposited—just as Soma is in the *camasa* cup.
Thus, upon that head, the multiform—the form of the universe—is placed and remains.

But what is that glory (*yaśas*)? Indeed, glory is the vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*), which are the multiform; the vital breaths are the senses such as hearing, and the Maruts, the winds, who are spread sevenfold among them—this is what the mantra declares.
Because it is the cause of the cognition of sound and other objects;
of that [unmanifest], the seven sages are the breaths whose nature is vibration,
and they alone are the sages.
The mantra speaks of these vital breaths: "Speech as the eighth, attaining union with Brahman. Being the eighth, it effects a communion with Brahman;
he states the reason for this: "For speech, as the eighth, attains union with Brahman. (3)
"But who were the seers sitting on the bank of that cup?
"These two indeed: Gautama and Bharadvāja."
This very one is Gautama, this one is Bharadvāja;
these two are Viśvāmitra and Jamadagni;
this very one is Viśvāmitra, this one is Jamadagni.
These two are Vasiṣṭha and Kaśyapa; this one is Vasiṣṭha, this one is Kaśyapa;
Speech itself is Atri.
For food is eaten by means of speech; "Autri" is indeed a name for "eater. He becomes the eater of everything.
All food becomes his who knows this thus. (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.2.4)
"These two, Gotama and Bharadvāja, are the ears"—this Gotama is the right one and this Bharadvāja is the left one, or vice versa.
Likewise, pointing out the eyes, he said: "These two, Viśvāmitra and Jamadagni, are [the eyes]"; Viśvāmitra is the right one and Jamadagni is the left one, or vice versa.
Pointing to these two nostrils, he said: "The right nostril is Vasiṣṭha,
and the left is Kaśyapa, as before."
Speech itself is Atri;
it is the seventh because of its connection with the act of eating.
For by speech food is eaten; therefore, "Atri" is indeed a well-known name for it, meaning "the eater" (attr) on account of its being an eater (attṛtva).
Although he is indeed the eater (*at-tṛ*), he is called "Atri" by means of an indirect expression (*parokṣeṇa*).

Through this knowledge of the etymological derivation of "Atri" in relation to this entire class of food belonging to the vital breath (*prāṇa*), one becomes an eater. He becomes an eater indeed; it is not the case that he is again encountered with food from another source—this is what is meant by the statement: "All food becomes his."
He who thus knows this true nature of the vital breath as it has been described—
he, having become this middle vital breath,
and being situated in the primary and secondary receptacles, becomes indeed the enjoyer.
It is not to be eaten;
the meaning is that it turns away from being edible. //4//
Thus ends the second Brāhmaṇa. //2//
START Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.3.1:
In this regard, it has been said that the vital breaths (prāṇas) are indeed truth; now, [we shall consider] those secret doctrines (upaniṣads) concerning the vital breaths.
These have been explained in connection with the Brahmopaniṣad: "These are your vital breaths. Now, what is their nature?
Or how is their reality established?

And it must be said that this Brāhmaṇa is commenced for the purpose of determining the true nature of the five elements— which are real and consist of effects and instruments— by means of which the reality of Brahman is intended to be pointed out through the removal of specific limiting adjuncts (upādhi) by the formula "not this, not this" (neti neti).
There are indeed two forms of Brahman.
Both the formed and the formless; both the mortal and the immortal;
and that which is stationary and that which moves.
Truth and renunciation. Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.3.1.

In that regard, Brahman is of two forms: that which is connected to the body and organs produced by the five elements, known as the manifest and the unmanifest, having the nature of mortal and immortal, consisting of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) produced therefrom, omniscient, omnipotent, and possessing a name;
and [the other form], which consists of action, agent, and fruit, being the locus of all worldly transactions.

That very Brahman, from which all distinctions of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) have departed, which is the object of perfect vision, unborn, undecaying, immortal, and fearless, being non-dual, is beyond the reach of both speech and mind; it is indicated by "not this, not this" (*neti neti*).
In that regard, Brahman is indicated by way of negation as "not this, not this."

These two indeed—here the word *vāva* is for the purpose of emphasis, meaning "only two"—are the two forms (*rūpe*) of Brahman, the Supreme Self; that is, by means of which two [forms], being superimposed through ignorance upon the formless Supreme Brahman, it is made to appear as having form.
What are those two? "The formed (*mūrta*) and indeed the formed alone," and likewise "the formless (*amūrta*) and indeed the formless alone. This is the meaning.
The two, the formed (*mūrta*) and the formless (*amūrta*), are determined as such by having their own specific attributes implicitly included within them.
What, then, are those attributes of the formed and the formless? They are stated as follows: "And mortal" (*martyam*) means subject to death.
And that which is immortal is the opposite of that;
and "stationary" refers to that which is limited and fixed after having undergone motion,
while "that which moves" refers to that which is all-pervading, unlimited, and the opposite of stationary.

The existent (*sat*) is that which possesses specific uncommon attributes by being distinguished from others; the non-existent (*asat*), however, is the opposite of that—that which is always fit for designation as "non-existent" (*atyat*) because it is beyond perception. //1//
In this regard, there is the "formed" (mūrta) and likewise the "formless" (amūrta), each distinguished by four specific attributes.
Among these, what are the specific attributes of the formed?
And what are the others?
This is analyzed:
it is that which is corporeal, other than wind and the intermediate space.
This is mortal; this is stationary; this is being.
Of this very one who has form, who is mortal, who is stationary, and who is existent—of him this is the essence: he who shines yonder.
For he is indeed the essence of the existent.
This is "embodied" (mūrta), meaning its parts have coalesced, its parts have entered into one another, and it is dense and compact.
What is that? It is that which is other. Other than what?
From the two remaining elements—wind and space—the triad of elements beginning with earth [is derived].
This is mortal: this triad of elements known as "the formed" (mūrta) is mortal, characterized by death. Why?
Because it is stationary (sthita).
For that which is delimited, when it comes into contact with another object, is contradicted by it—just as a jar is [contradicted] by a pillar, a wall, and so forth.
Likewise, that which is corporeal, situated, and delimited is mortal because of its contradiction with other objects due to its relation to them; this, being qualified, possesses uncommon attributes.
For that which is indeed limited, being limited, is mortal; therefore it is embodied;
or, because it is embodied, it is mortal.
Because it is mortal, it is established; because it is established, it exists.

Therefore, since these four properties do not deviate from one another, their relationship as qualifier and qualified, as well as their relationship as cause and effect, may be demonstrated as desired.

In every respect, however, the three elements (bhūtas) characterized by the fourfold attributes constitute the formal (mūrta) form of Brahman. Among these, when one attribute is grasped, the others are necessarily grasped as well; thus he says: "of this formal [Brahman], of this mortal..."
Of this which is established, of this which exists— that is, of the triad of elements characterized by these four qualities— this is the essence (rasa), meaning the quintessence (sāra).
For Savitṛ is the most essential of the three elements;
these three elements have him as their essence,
since they possess the specific qualities of form that are produced and differentiated by him.
This is the form of the cosmic (ādhidevika) effect: that which is this orb of the sun which shines;
for it is understood as the essence of the three elements that have come into being, since this embodied sun shines.
And [the term] *sāriṣṭha*.
We shall now explain that which is the divine instrument (*adhidaivika-karaṇa*) within the mandala. //2//
Now,
the formless consists of wind and the intermediate space.
This is the immortal;
this is that which is; this is yonder.
Of this formless, immortal, and undecaying [ātman], of that which is beyond this, this is the essence: namely, the person who is in this orb.
For he is indeed the essence of that which is beyond this.
Thus far with respect to the divine. (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.3.3)
Now, as for the formless: next, the formless is being described.
Wind and the intermediate space—these two remaining elements—are immortal because they are formless; they are non-static.
Therefore, that which is not contradicted by anything,
which is immortal and characterized by non-death—
this is what is opposite to the state of being established [in saṃsāra].
It is all-pervasive and undivided,
because this [reality] has no specific distinctions that can be differentiated from others.
Therefore, "that" (*tyat*)—just as before—is precisely that which is fit to be designated by a remote term.
Of this amorphous, of this immortal, of this "that" which possesses these four qualifying attributes, this is the essence (*rasa*). What is it? That which...
This person within this orb, consisting of the instruments [of perception], is designated as Hiraṇyagarbha, the Prāṇa;
he is the essence (*rasa*) of the two formless elements, the most excellent extract (*sāriṣṭha*), as previously described.
And these two formless elements, having him—the Person—as their essence, manifest from the Undifferentiated (*avyākṛta*) for the purpose of originating the subtle body (*liṅga*) of Hiraṇyagarbha.
Therefore, because it exists for that purpose, that pair of elements has that as its essence.

For this is their "savor" (rasa): since the Person residing in the orb is not perceived apart from the orb, and he is the essence of the pair of elements, there is thus a similarity between the Person residing in the orb and the pair of elements.
Therefore, it is appropriate to employ a reason as something well-known, namely: "for this is its essence" (*rasa*).
Some maintain that "essence" (*rasa*) means the cause, the conscious self consisting of the knowledge of Hiraṇyagarbha.
And in that context, it is said that the action of the conscious self consisting of the knowledge of Hiraṇyagarbha is the impeller of both wind and the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*).

That action, having the wind and the atmosphere as its support, becomes the impeller of the other elements; because it is the impeller of the wind and the atmosphere through its own action, it is said that their "essence" (rasa) is the cause.
That is not so, because [action] is not equal to a material essence (mūrtarasa).

The essence of the three material elements is seen to be a material sphere, which belongs to the same genus as those three elements and is not conscious; likewise, it is logical that the essence of the two immaterial elements should also consist of something immaterial, belonging to the same genus as them,
because the manner of the scriptural discourse is the same.

Just as the two categories, the formed and the formless, are distinguished as possessing four attributes each, so too is the distinction between the possessed-taste and the taste itself appropriate by the same logic; it is not a partial or inconsistent application.
If it is argued that even in the case of a material object (*mūrtarasa*), the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) is intended to be conscious,
this is stating too little; for in every instance, both the material and the immaterial are intended to be of the nature of Brahman.

If it is argued that the word *puruṣa* (person) is inappropriate for something insentient, we say no; for the word *puruṣa* is observed to be applied to a sacrificial symbol (*liṅga*) characterized by specific parts such as wings and a tail.
As it is said: "Being thus, we shall not be able to procreate offspring; let us make these seven persons into one person."
Because the word "puruṣa" is used in such passages as, "They made these seven puruṣas into one puruṣa," and in other Vedic texts regarding those consisting of the essence of food and so forth;
thus, the conclusion "so far with respect to the deities" (ity adhidaivatam) is stated for the purpose of introducing the division concerning the self (adhyātma). //3//
Now,
with reference to the self:
that which is corporeal is this very thing, namely whatever is other than the vital breath and that space which is within the self.
This is mortal; this is stationary; this is being.
Of this very embodied one, of this mortal one, of this stationary one, of this existent one, the eye is the essence;
for it is the essence of the existent.
Now, the internal division between the formed (*mūrta*) and the formless (*amūrta*) is being stated: what is that which is formed? It is this very [body]. And what is this?

Whatever is other than the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the wind (*vāyu*), and whatever is this space (*ākāśa*) or void (*kha*) within the self (*ātman*), as well as the vital breath residing in the body—excluding these two, whatever else constitutes the origin of the body.
The passage beginning with "This is the mortal" and so forth is otherwise the same as the previous one.
For this [ether] is the essence (*rasa*) of that Being—namely, the eye;
it is the essence, the core substance, of the internal effect which constitutes the body.

Therefore, by means of that essence, this entire body becomes possessed of essence, just as [the body] is with respect to its presiding deity through the solar orb. Furthermore, because of their primacy, it is the eyes alone that first come into being, as indicated by the scriptural sign: "From heat, the essence flowed forth as fire."
For the eye is fiery; this is its essence;
for the eye is indeed fiery.
This triad of elements is the internal essence; for it is the "taste" (rasa) of that which exists—this is the meaning of the reason for its being the essence of material form. //4//
Now, as for the formless: the vital breath and that space which is within the self—
this is the immortal.
This is that;
this is yonder.
Of this formless one, of this immortal one, of this moving one, of this yonder one, this is the essence: namely, this person who is in the right eye.
For this, indeed, is its essence.
Now, that which is formless is being described:
the two remaining elements, the vital breath (prāṇa), and this space within the self (antarātman)—
this is the formless.
The rest is as before.
This is the essence and the core of this [world]:
namely, this person who is in the right eye. The specific mention of "in the right eye" is for the sake of distinction.
Because it is directly perceived in the scriptures;
for the specific presiding authority of the *liṅga* over the right eye is directly perceived in the scriptures, as such usage is seen in all the Vedas, [as in the passage]:
"For this is its essence."
As before, because it is not specifically perceived [as having a distinct form], the meaning of the reason is that its essence consists precisely in its being incorporeal. //5//
START Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.3.6:

The division of the two limiting adjuncts (upādhi) of Brahman—namely, the formed (mūrta) and the formless (amūrta)—which are denoted by the word "Satya," has been explained through their distinction as effects and instruments, both with respect to the body (adhyātma) and the deities (adhidaivata).
Now, therefore—
Now, the form of this very person is like a garment dyed with turmeric, like white wool, like a cochineal insect, like the flame of a fire, like a lotus, like a sudden flash of lightning. Indeed,
the splendor of one who knows this becomes like a sudden flash of lightning.
Now, therefore, follows the instruction: "Not this, not this.
For there is nothing else higher than this "not this.
Now, its name is "the Truth of truth."
The vital breaths are indeed truth;
he is their truth. (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.3.6)

We shall now describe the form of this very person, which consists of the instruments—the subtle body (*liṅga*)—composed of latent impressions (*vāsanā*). This form is produced by the conjunction of the material and immaterial latent impressions with consciousness;
it is manifold, like a painting on a cloth or a wall, resembling a magical illusion (*māyā*), a feat of sorcery (*indrajāla*), or a mirage (*mṛgatṛṣṇikā*), and is the locus of all delusion.
It is here that the nihilists (*vaināśika*), who are proponents of consciousness-only (*vijñānavādin*), have gone astray, asserting that "the Self is merely this much."
The Naiyāyikas and Vaiśeṣikas agree that this very form of latent impression (*vāsanā*) is a quality (*guṇa*) of the substance (*dravya*) that is the self (*ātman*), like the color of a cloth.

The Sāṅkhyas maintain that this three-fold nature (*triguṇa*), which exists for the sake of the self, is independent and functions by taking recourse in *pradhāna* with the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*) as its cause.
Even some who consider themselves followers of the Upaniṣads construct a system, [asserting] that there is one aggregate consisting of the formed (*mūrta*) and the formless (*amūrta*).
The supreme is the aggregate of the Self (paramātmarāśi);

distinct from those two is this third, the intermediate one, namely the collection of knowledge, action, and prior cognition (vidyā-karma-pūrvaprajñā-samudāya), together with the agent and enjoyer consisting of consciousness (vijñānamaya) as awakened by Ajātaśatru;
and the instigator is the aggregate of action (karmarāśi).
The previously mentioned aggregate of beings, both manifest and unmanifest, is the object to be employed and the means as well.
In that regard, they enter into debate with the logicians;
having asserted that this aggregate of karma has the *liṅga* (the subtle body) as its substratum, they then recoil from it out of fear of being identified as Sāṅkhyas.
The entire mass of karma, like fragrance residing in a flower, continues to reside in the oil within the container even after the flower has been removed;
similarly, even when separated from the *liṅga* (the subtle body), it takes refuge in a portion of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).
That portion of the Supreme Self, though inherently devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*), becomes possessed of qualities (*saguṇa*) by means of the quality of karma that has come from elsewhere.
They also follow the view of the Vaiśeṣikas, that the conscious self (vijñānātman) is the agent, the enjoyer, that which is bound, and that which is liberated;
and that mass of karma is adventitious to the mass of elements,
for the self is by its very nature devoid of qualities, being a mere portion of the Supreme Self.

Ignorance (*avidyā*) arises from itself; though not adventitious, it is a non-self-attribute (*anātma-dharma*), like saline soil (*ūṣara*). Following this conception, they conform to the mind of the Sāṅkhya.
They regard all of this as delightful through a conception of consistency with logicians, yet they perceive the established doctrine of the Upaniṣads as being in contradiction with all logic. How so?

Thus, the defects— such as the impossibility of transmigration, being subject to wounds, and the experience of the fruits of karma in a specific location for the Supreme Self, as well as its being a transmigrating soul with wounds— have already been stated regarding its being limited (sāvayavatva).
Furthermore, if there were an eternal difference [between them], the oneness of the individual self (vijñānātman) with the Supreme would be impossible.

If it is argued that the subtle body (*liṅga*) itself is [the locus], then— since it is merely a conceptualized spatial location of the Supreme Self (Paramātman), like the space within a jar, a water-pot, or a hole in the ground—
it would follow that even upon separation from the subtle body, the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) would still reside in the location of the Supreme Self,
and ignorance (*avidyā*) would arise spontaneously, like saline soil; such a conceptualization is simply untenable.

Furthermore, it is not possible even for the mind to conceive that a latent impression (*vāsanā*) moves to another object apart from its location; nor do the scriptural texts support this, as seen in passages such as: "Desire, resolve, and doubt," "For forms are indeed in the heart," "It meditates, as it were; it trembles, as it were," "The desires that dwell in his heart," and "For then one has crossed beyond all sorrows of the heart.
It is not proper to assume a meaning other than what is heard in these scriptures.
Since these [passages] are intended solely for the purpose of establishing that the self is the Supreme Brahman,
and since all the Upaniṣads exhaust their meaning in this much alone,
therefore all those who are skilled in imagining meanings other than what is stated in the Śruti interpret the meaning of the Upaniṣads otherwise.
Nevertheless, if it were the meaning of the Veda, let it be so; I have no aversion to that.
Furthermore, the statement "There are indeed two forms of Brahman" would not be consistent with the position that there are three groups [of elements].
But when the formed and the formless, as well as the latent impressions produced by them— these two forms— and Brahman as the third form exist,
and there is no other fourth entity in between, then this restrictive determination is appropriate.

"There are only two forms of Brahman"; otherwise, it would have to be imagined that these are the forms of the individual self (vijñānātman), which is but a portion of Brahman, or that they belong to the Supreme Self (paramātman) by way of the individual self.
And in that case, the dual number in "rūpe eva" (only the two forms) would be inconsistent;

rather, the plural form "rūpāṇi" (the forms) would be more appropriate along with the latent impressions (*vāsanā*), since there are the two—the formed and the formless—and the latent impressions as the third.
Or else, the formed and the formless alone are the forms of the Supreme Self.

If it is argued that the latent impressions (vāsanās) belong to the conscious self (vijñānātman), then this mode of expression— that the Supreme Self undergoes modification through the medium of the conscious self— would be meaningless, since the fact that the latent impressions also operate through the medium of the conscious self remains unchanged. Furthermore, it cannot be conceived in its primary sense that one entity undergoes modification through the medium of another entity.
Furthermore, the conscious self (*vijñānātman*) is not a different entity from the supreme self (*paramātman*),
for such a conception would result in the abandonment of established doctrine.
Therefore, these and similar conceptions, arising solely from the minds of those who are deluded regarding the meaning of the Veda, are outside the scope of the sacred syllables.
For the meaning of the Veda is neither outside of the letters nor does it assist the meaning of the Veda, because the Veda’s authority regarding its own meaning is independent [of anything else];
therefore, the conceptualization of three heaps is inconsistent.
The person who was introduced as being within the right eye in the context of the internal self (*adhyātma*),

and as "this person who is in this orb" in the context of the divine (*adhidaiva*)— he alone is referred to by the word "his," because he is the subject under discussion; he is the essence (*rasa*) of that which is formless, and not the one consisting of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*).
Now, why might these forms not belong to that which consists of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*) alone?
For that which consists of consciousness is also the subject under discussion,
and the word "his" (*tasya*) refers back to the subject at hand.
It is not so, because that which consists of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*) is intended to be made known as being formless (*arūpin*);

for if these forms, such as the saffron-colored robe and so forth, belonged to that very one consisting of consciousness, there would be no instruction regarding it as having an indefinable nature by means of "not this, not this" (*neti neti*).
[Objection: But surely this instruction refers to something else, and not to that which consists of consciousness?

No, because at the end of the sixth [chapter] there is a concluding summary: “By what, my dear, would one know the knower? Having introduced the one consisting of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*), and having made the promise, “I shall make him known as ‘not this, not this’,” this [promise] becomes meaningful.

For if it were intended to make known the very nature of the self of the one consisting of consciousness—which is beyond all empirical transaction and in which all specific adjuncts have been destroyed—then this promise would be meaningful; for once he has been made known by that [teaching], he would know the Self, thinking, “I am Brahman.”
One attains the culmination of the teachings and fears nothing from anywhere.

However, if it were that the one consisting of consciousness is one thing and the one designated as "not this, not this" is another, then [one would think] "Brahman is that other thing, and I am someone else."
Otherwise, a misconception would have been grasped, rather than [the realization] "I am indeed Brahman; I have known myself.
Therefore, these forms belong specifically to the symbolic person (liṅgapuruṣa), as indicated by the words "of this very one" (tasya haitasya).
And when the true nature of the Supreme Self— the truth of truths— is to be described, truth must be explained in its entirety;
and since the specific forms of truth are the latent impressions (*vāsanās*), these forms of theirs are now being stated.

These are the forms of this aforementioned person, who is of the nature of the subtle body (*liṅga-ātman*). What are they? They are stated as follows: just as in the world there is *māhārajana*, which is cloth dyed with *haridrā* (turmeric), so too [is this person].
In this way, through contact with objects such as women, a corresponding form of latent impression (*vāsanā*) arises in the mind in the form of passion,
by which that person is said to be "colored" (*rakta*), just like a cloth or similar object.
And just as in the world there is a pale woolen garment—
This includes wool, sheep’s wool, and so forth;
and just as that is white, so too is another form of latent impression (*vāsanā*).
And just as the indragopa insect is intensely red in the world,
such is the nature of its latent impression (*vāsanā*);
in some cases, there is a gradation of passion depending on specific objects.
In some cases, it depends on the mental activity of a person;
just as in the world the flame of a fire is brilliant,
so in some instances it takes the form of a latent impression (*vāsanā*) for someone.
Just as a white lotus,
so too does the form of latent impressions (vāsanā) belong to someone;
just as it is once liberated from [defilement].
Just as in the world a single flash of lightning illuminates everything,
so too, in view of the increase of the illumination of knowledge, a certain form of latent impression (*vāsanā*) arises for someone.
Of these forms of latent impressions, there is no beginning, end, middle, or number.
Neither place, time, nor cause can be determined, because the latent impressions (vāsanā) are innumerable and the causes of those impressions are infinite.
And so he will state in the sixth [chapter]: "Consisting of this, consisting of that," and so forth.
Therefore, the illustrations such as "like a garment dyed with safflower" are not intended to determine the specific nature or number [of latent impressions];
rather, they are for the purpose of showing the types, meaning that the forms of latent impressions are of such a kind.

As for what was stated at the end regarding its nature as a latent impression (*vāsanā*)— namely, that it is "like a single flash of lightning"— it is said that when Hiraṇyagarbha emerges from the unmanifest (*avyākṛta*), his manifestation occurs all at once, like a flash of lightning.
For one who knows that form of Hiraṇyagarbha’s latent impression, it is like a single flash of lightning.
The two particles *ha* and *vai* serve the purpose of emphasis;
the meaning is that his glory and renown become exactly thus—
