just as they are for Hiraṇyagarbha— for him who knows this aforementioned final form consisting of latent impressions (*vāsanā*).

Having thus described the nature of Truth (satya) in its entirety, this section concerning Brahman is commenced for the purpose of ascertaining the specific nature of that which we have called "the Truth of Truth. Now— immediately after the description of the nature of Truth—
since only that which is the Truth of Truth remains, therefore we shall describe the nature of the Truth of Truth.
The instruction regarding Brahman is its definition.
What, then, is that definition? It is said: the definition is "not this, not this" (neti neti).
Now, how is it that by these two words, "not this, not this" (*neti neti*), the "Truth of Truths" is intended to be pointed out?
It is said: by the exclusion of all specific limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).
In that [Reality] there is no distinction whatsoever—neither name, nor form, nor action, nor difference, nor genus, nor quality.
For it is by means of those [attributes] that the application of words occurs;
yet there is no distinction whatsoever among them with respect to Brahman,
and therefore it cannot be pointed out as "this is that."

Just as in the world one points out [an object] by saying, "That white, moving, horned thing is a cow," so too is Brahman pointed out by means of superimposed name, form, and action through such words as, "Brahman is consciousness and bliss" (vijñānam ānandam brahma), and "The Self, which is Brahman, is a mass of consciousness alone" (vijñānaghana eva brahmātmeti). However, when its own true nature (svarūpa) is intended to be pointed out;

When it is devoid of all specific adjuncts (upādhi), it cannot be designated by any means whatsoever; at that time, this is the only method: namely, the designation "not this, not this" (neti neti) by way of negating all possible designations.
And these two "na"s are for the purpose of repetition and pervasion; whatever is encountered is each and every one negated.
This being so, the suspicion regarding Brahman that was not explicitly mentioned is thereby removed.
For otherwise, if the two subjects under discussion were negated by the two "nots," and no Brahman other than those two negated subjects were specified,
the doubt— "What indeed is it like?"— would not be removed.
Furthermore, that instruction would be purposeless,
as it does not bring about the desire to know in the person; and the sentence "I shall make you know Brahman" would have its meaning left incomplete.

But when the desire to know [the distinctions of] all directions, time, and so forth has ceased through the removal of all limiting adjuncts (upādhi), then— like a single mass of salt— the mass of consciousness (prajñānaghana) is of one taste,
without interior or exterior, the reality of reality; at that point, the desire to know ceases entirely with the realization "I am Brahman," and wisdom becomes established in the Self alone.
Therefore, the two negations "not this, not this" (*neti neti*) are for the purpose of repetition (*vīpsā*).
Now, having prepared such a great effort, is it indeed appropriate to define Brahman in this way?
Certainly; why?
For indeed, because of this— "not so,
not so"— the two instances of the word "iti" indicate the two occurrences of the negative particle (*na*) which are the objects of pervasion.
Just as when one says "village after village is delightful," there is no further specification beyond that;
therefore, this alone is the description of Brahman.
As it has been said: "Its secret name (upaniṣad) is 'the truth of truth'"—in this manner, that which is the truth of truth is the Supreme Brahman;
therefore, it is rightly stated that this is the name of Brahman.
"Name" is indeed "nāmadheya" (that which is called by name). What is that?
It is the truth of truth. The vital breaths (prāṇas) are indeed truth, and he is their truth. //6//
Thus ends the third Brāhmaṇa. //3//
"Let one worship [the Self] as 'the Self' alone;
that very reality of the Self is what is to be reached within all this."

Since the relationship and purpose have been stated in the context of explaining the sentence introduced as "That which is dearer than a son," etc.— namely, "He knew only himself as 'I am Brahman,' therefore he became all that"—
it has thus been set forth that the inner self (pratyagātman) is the subject matter of the knowledge of Brahman.

Furthermore, the subject matter of ignorance (avidyā) begins with the words, "He who thinks 'that one is one and I am another' does not know," and extends to the definition of the means and ends accomplished by the fivefold ritual acts, which are based on the distinctions of the four castes and so forth.

Samsara, which consists of name-and-form (nāmarūpa) and action (karman), has a nature that is both determinate (vyākṛta) and indeterminate (avyākṛta), like a seed and its sprout; it is summarized as: "This triad, indeed, is name, form, and action.

The upward progression characterized by excellence, culminating in the world of Brahman (brahmaloka), and the downward state, culminating in stationary beings (sthāvara), have already been demonstrated previously in the passage beginning with, "There are two [kinds of people]," and so forth.

Thinking, "How indeed may one who is detached from this entire sphere of ignorance become qualified for the knowledge of Brahman, whose object is the inner Self (pratyagātman)? the entire sphere of ignorance was summarized in the third chapter.

In the fourth chapter, however, having introduced the subject of the knowledge of Brahman—the inner Self—with the words "I shall tell you of Brahman" and "I shall make Brahman known," that Brahman—unique, non-dual, devoid of all distinctions, and free from the nature of action, agent, and fruit—is made known by means of the negation of all phenomenal attributes expressible by words such as "truth" through the formula "not this, not this" (neti neti).

Renunciation is intended to be enjoined as an auxiliary to this knowledge of Brahman, because the fivefold ritual action characterized by wife, son, wealth, and so forth, which falls within the domain of ignorance, is not a means for attaining the Self; for indeed, a means intended for one purpose, when employed for the sake of achieving a different result, becomes counterproductive.
For neither running nor walking is the means for the cessation of hunger and thirst;
indeed, the means such as a son and so forth are taught in scripture as the means for attaining the world of men, the world of the ancestors, and the world of the gods,
but not as the means for attaining the Self.
And because they are specified as such;
furthermore, these rites are not prescribed for one who knows Brahman,
since they are heard to be optional— “This much indeed is desire.”
Furthermore, because the knower of Brahman has attained all desires, desire is impossible for one who has attained all desires;
as the Śruti says: "For us, this Self is the world.
However, some describe even knowers of Brahman as being connected with longing.

They have not heard the Bṛhadāraṇyaka; they have not heard the distinction made by the Śruti between the domain of the ignorant—characterized by the desire for sons and so forth—and the domain of knowledge, which begins with “For us, this Self is this world” and concludes with “What shall we do with offspring?”; thus, the division established by the Śruti has not been heard by them.

Furthermore, while knowledge— which consists in the sublation of all actions, factors of action, and results— is present, they have not understood the contradiction characterized by the impossibility of ignorance existing together with its effects;
nor have they heard the words of Vyāsa.
Conflict is the contrary operation of action and knowledge, which consist respectively of ignorance and wisdom:
"Regarding this statement of the Vedas, 'Perform action' and 'Renounce action,' what goal do they reach through knowledge, and what goal do they go to by means of action?"
“I truly wish to hear this; may your lordship explain it to me:
how is it that these two exist in mutual opposition and hostility?
To him who had thus questioned, he replied: “A living being is bound by karma and liberated by knowledge.”
Therefore, the ascetics who see the further shore do not perform ritual actions.
Thus, such contradictions have been demonstrated.
Therefore, the knowledge of Brahman, when accompanied by other means of accomplishment, is not the means for achieving the goal of human life,
because of all these contradictions.

Since it is determined at the conclusion of the sixth chapter that "this alone is the means for attaining immortality," renunciation— characterized by the relinquishing of all means— is enjoined as an auxiliary, on the grounds that it is the very accomplishment of the human goal independently of other means.
And from an indicative mark (*liṅga*), it appears that Yājñavalkya, being a performer of ritual action, renounced the world;
for he taught the knowledge of Brahman as a means for attaining immortality to Maitreyī—who was herself devoid of the means for ritual action—and because of his statements censuring wealth.
For if ritual action were the means to immortality, then the fivefold ritual action achievable through wealth would [be the means].
Thus, such a statement of censure would be undesirable;
however, if it is the action that one intends to cause to be abandoned, then the censure of its means is appropriate.

Furthermore, because there is a sublation of the notions of caste, stage of life, and so forth— which serve as the basis for authority over ritual action— as seen in such passages as, "He deprives him of his Brahman-hood" and "He deprives him of his Kshatriya-hood," an injunction finds no footing; for when the notions of selfhood associated with Brahmin, Kshatriya, and so on are sublated,
there is no objective basis for an injunction such as "this must be done by a Brahmin" or "this must be done by a Kshatriya."

For that very person whose cognition regarding the Self—consisting of Brahminhood, Kṣatriyahood, and so forth—has been sublated, there follows, by virtue of the renunciation of that cognition, the renunciation of its effects, namely ritual actions and the means for performing those actions; this renunciation being thus established as a matter of course.
Therefore, with the desire to prescribe renunciation as an ancillary to the knowledge of the Self, this narrative is commenced.
"Maitreyī," Yājñavalkya said, "I am indeed about to depart from this place.
Come, let me make a final settlement between you and Kātyāyanī."
"Maitreyī," said Yājñavalkya— the sage named Yājñavalkya addressed his own wife Maitreyī— "I am about to depart, O dear one (are), that is,
I am going upward to another stage of life called wandering mendicancy (pārivrājya)."
I desire to go upward from this state of household life, from this station, from this stage of life.
Therefore, I seek your permission to kill her;
furthermore, I shall bring about an end to your relationship with this second wife, Kātyāyanī,
severing my connection with both of you through your husband by dividing the property.
Having shared my wealth with you both, I shall depart. //1//
Maitreyī said: "If, O Venerable Sir, this entire earth filled with wealth were mine, would I become immortal by means of that?
"No," said Yājñavalkya.
"Let your life be just like the life of those who possess material means; however, there is no hope for immortality through wealth. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.2)
Thus addressed, she said: "If— if" (the word *anu* being used here in the sense of deliberation)— "this earth belongs to me, O Bhagoḥ— O Venerable One."
Even if the entire earth, surrounded by the oceans, were filled with wealth and riches—how so?
The sense is that it could not be so in any way; this is either an objection (*ākṣepa*) or a question (*praśna*).

The connection with the remote [clause] is as follows: "By means of that ritual action, such as the *agnihotra* and so forth, which is to be accomplished by wealth sufficient to fill the earth, could I become immortal?
Yājñavalkya replied: "How so? If this is intended as a challenge (*ākṣepārtha*), it is not an expression of assent; thus Yājñavalkya said, "No. If "How so? is intended as a challenge...
"It is not approval," said Yājñavalkya.
If it were for the purpose of answering a question, they would certainly not be immortal; what then?

Just as in the world the life of those who possess means and instruments is endowed with the enjoyment of the means for happiness, even so would your life be; yet there is no hope for immortality, even in thought, through wealth or through action accomplished by wealth. //2//
Maitreyī said: "What should I do with that by which I would not become immortal?
Tell me only that which you know, O Venerable One."
Maitreyī said:
Having been addressed thus, Maitreyī replied, "If it were so, what would I do with that wealth by which I would not become immortal?"
Whatever means for attaining immortality the Blessed One knows exclusively, please tell that very means for attaining immortality to me. //3//
Yājñavalkya said: "O lady, you have always been dear to us, and you speak what is dear. Come, sit down."
"I shall explain it to you;
but while I am explaining, reflect deeply upon it. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.4)
Yājñavalkya said:
When that means for attaining immortality which is accomplished through wealth had thus been rejected,
Yājñavalkya, satisfied with the fulfillment of his own intention, spoke.
He said:
"O Maitreyī, alas! [he spoke thus] out of compassion], you who were already dear to us before, now speak only what is pleasing and agreeable to our hearts."
Therefore, come here, sit down, and I shall explain—namely, I shall tell you that knowledge of the Self which is desired by you and is the means to immortality.
Furthermore, as I am explaining—that is, while I am performing the exposition—you should practice *nididhyāsana*, desiring to meditate with certainty upon the meaning of my words. //4//

He said: "Truly, it is not out of love for the husband that the husband is dear, but it is out of love for the Self that the husband is dear. Truly, it is not out of love for the wife that the wife is dear, but it is out of love for the Self that the wife is dear."

"Verily, it is not out of love for their sons that sons are dear, but it is out of love for oneself that sons are dear. Verily, it is not out of love for wealth that wealth is dear, but it is out of love for oneself that wealth is dear. Verily, it is not out of love for the sacred word (*brahman*) that the sacred word is dear, but it is out of love for oneself that the sacred word is dear."
Verily, it is not out of love for the ruling power that the ruling power is dear; rather, it is out of love for the Self that the ruling power is dear.

Verily, it is not out of love for the worlds that the worlds are dear; rather, it is out of love for the Self that the worlds are dear. Verily, it is not out of love for the gods that the gods are dear; rather, it is out of love for the Self that the gods are dear.
"Verily, it is not for the sake of beings that beings are dear, but for the sake of the Self that beings are dear.
Verily, it is not for the sake of everything that everything is dear, but for the sake of the Self that everything is dear.
Therefore, the Self, O Maitreyī, should be seen, heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon."
"Verily, my dear, by seeing, hearing, thinking, and knowing the Self, all this is known."
He said this: desiring to teach detachment as the means to immortality, he produces a dispassion toward wife, husband, son, and so forth, for the sake of renouncing them.
"Na vai"—the word *vai* is used here to recall what is well-known;
indeed, this is already well-established in the world.

The husband is not dear to the wife for the sake of the husband—that is, for his own purpose—but rather the husband is dear to the wife only for the sake of the self. Likewise, "Verily, the wife is not [dear] for the sake of the wife," and so forth; the rest is the same.
"Verily, it is not for the sake of sons, nor for the sake of wealth, nor for the sake of the Veda."
Nor indeed, O friend, does it belong to the Kṣatriya,
nor indeed to the gods, nor indeed to the beings.
Nor, indeed, is there a statement regarding everything [as being the means to bliss], each preceding one being mentioned according to its proximity as a means to joy;
for in each such case, there arises a greater degree of detachment from it.
The inclusion of the word "all" is intended to encompass both what has been stated and what has not been stated.
Therefore, this is well-known in the world: the self alone is dear, and nothing else.
This is what was introduced in the passage, "This is dearer than a son."
This has been explained in detail as being analogous to its function.
Therefore, because it is a means for attaining pleasure for the Self, pleasure elsewhere is secondary;
it is primary only in the Self.
Therefore, indeed, my dear, the Self must be seen— that is, it is worthy of being seen and must be brought within the range of vision;
it must first be heard from the teacher and from the sacred tradition.
Afterwards, it should be reflected upon through reasoning; thereafter, it should be meditated upon through contemplation, meaning it should be contemplated with certainty.
For in this way, it becomes truly seen, by means of the instruments of hearing, reflection, and contemplation having been accomplished.
When the notions of oneness have been attained, then right vision (samyagdarśana) regarding the subject of the oneness of Brahman becomes established;
it does not arise otherwise by mere hearing alone.

That which consists of the Brahmin, the Kṣatriya, and so forth—characterized by caste and stage of life (*varṇāśrama*), caused by action, having as its object the notions superimposed by the knowledge of the Self, consisting of action, agent, and fruit, and being the object of the notion of ignorance—is for the purpose of destroying that [ignorance] like [the illusion of] a snake in a rope.
Therefore, he says: "Verily, Maitreyī, when the Self alone has been seen, heard, thought upon, and known, all this becomes known and understood. (5)
Now, one might object: "How can one thing be known when something else is known?
This is not a fault;
for there is indeed nothing whatsoever that exists apart from the Self.
If it were something else, it would not be known; but there is nothing else,
for the Self alone is everything.

Therefore, when the Self is known, everything becomes known. But how is it that the Self alone is everything?
