Brahman deserts him who knows Brahman as other than the Self; the Kṣatra deserts him who knows the Kṣatra as other than the Self;
the worlds desert him who knows the worlds as other than the Self.
The gods desert him who knows the gods as other than the Self;
the beings desert him who knows the beings as other than the Self;
everything deserts him who knows everything as other than the Self.
This is the Brahman, this is the Kṣatra, these are the worlds, these are the gods, these are all beings—this whole world is that which is this Self.
The Brahman—the Brāhmaṇa caste—would cast that person away, would reject him, would exclude him; who?
He who knows it as something other than the Self, apart from the nature of the Self, thinking, "This Brāhmaṇa caste is not the Self itself"—him she (the caste) would cast away.
"The Brāhmaṇa caste beholds me as being of the nature of the non-self;
for the Supreme Self is indeed the Self of all. Likewise, the Kṣatra—the Kṣatriya caste—"
Likewise, the worlds, the gods, the beings, and everything.

All those things which have been enumerated as "This is Brahman" are nothing but the Self— that very Self which is the subject under discussion, described as "this Self which is to be seen, to be heard."
Since it is born from the Self, merges into the Self alone, and consists of the Self during the time of its existence—
because it cannot be apprehended apart from the Self—
the Self alone is everything. //6//
But how, then, can it be grasped that all this is indeed the Self alone?
It is understood that because pure consciousness (cinmātra) pervades everything, everything has the very nature of consciousness.
In this regard, an illustration is stated:
In this regard, an illustration is stated: in the world, it is observed that whatever is not perceived apart from its own nature is indeed identical with that [nature].
Just as, when a drum is being beaten, one would not be able to grasp the external sounds; but by grasping the drum, or the striking of the drum, the sound is grasped. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.7)
The phrase "as that" (*sa yathā-sa*) is an illustration; it refers to how, in the world, when a drum, a kettledrum, or the like is being struck— that is,
beaten with a stick or similar instrument— it [is not perceived individually].

One would not be able to grasp— that is, to perceive— the external sounds, which are specific instances of sound distinguished from the general category of drum-sound; however, by grasping the drum itself, one perceives that "these are drum-sounds."
Specific sounds are apprehended because they do not exist apart from the generality of the sound of a drum,
or rather, apart from the striking of the drum.
The striking of the drum is the cause of the cognition;

by the apprehension of the general property of sound as distinguished by the striking of the drum, the particulars inherent in it are apprehended, for those particulars cannot be apprehended by being separated from that [general property].
Because they lack any specific form, no distinct entity whatsoever is perceived apart from consciousness in either the dreaming or waking states;
therefore, it is logical that these two states do not exist apart from consciousness. //7//

Just as, when a conch is being blown, one would not be able to grasp external sounds, yet by grasping the conch or the blower of the conch, the sound is grasped; even so, when a conch is being blown—that is, joined with sound and filled—one would not be able to grasp external sounds, and so forth, as described previously. (BrhUp 2.4.8)
Just as when a lute is being played, one cannot grasp the external sounds; rather, by grasping the lute itself, or the lute-player, the sound is grasped. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.9)
Likewise, "for the lute being played" means for the *vīṇā* being played.

The employment of numerous examples here is for the purpose of making known the multiplicity of universals (*sāmānya*); for there are indeed many diverse universals and particulars, both conscious and unconscious, which, through a successive process of inclusion, find their subsumption within a single Great Universal, the Mass of Consciousness (*prajñānaghana*).
How, indeed, is this to be demonstrated?

Just as the general and specific qualities of the sounds of a drum, a conch, and a lute are included within the universal property of "soundness," so too, during the period of manifestation (sthitikāla), because the general and specific qualities are not distinct from it, the oneness of Brahman can be understood. //9//
Thus, at the time of origination, it can be understood that prior to origination there was Brahman alone;
just as in the case of fire, prior to the separation of its sparks, smoke, embers, and flames, there is only fire, and thus the oneness of fire exists.

Thus, it is logical to hold that prior to its arising, the world—though differentiated by name and form—is indeed a mass of consciousness alone; this is stated as follows: "Just as, my dear, from a fire kindled with damp fuel various clouds of smoke issue forth, even so, verily, these—the Rigveda, the Yajurveda, the Samaveda, the Atharvangirasa, and the Itihasa—are the breath of this great Being."
The Purāṇas, the Vedas, the Upaniṣads, the verses, the aphorisms, the expositions, and the commentaries—these are indeed his breaths. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.10)
Just as in the case of fire with wet fuel— that is,
fire kindled by wet fuel is "fire with wet fuel"—
from that [it follows]:
From the fire that has been kindled, various smokes arise;
"various" means of many different kinds.
The mention of "smoke" is intended to illustrate sparks and so forth as well.
Smoke, sparks, and so forth issue forth and go out;
just as in this illustration,
O Maitreyī, this [world] is the breath of that great being who is the subject under discussion, the Supreme Self.
It is like a breath exhaled;
just as a person’s breath occurs without any effort, so it is with this, O venerable one.
What is that which was born from it like a breath? It is said to be: the Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, the Sāmaveda, and the Atharvāṅgirasa—the fourfold collection of mantras.
*Itihāsa* refers to the dialogue between Urvaśī and Purūravas and so forth; *Brāhmaṇa* refers specifically to such texts as “Urvaśī, indeed, was an Apsaras” and so on;
*Purāṇa* refers to such passages as “In the beginning, this was non-existent (*asad*)” and so on;
and *Vidyā* refers to the knowledge of the gods, such as the Veda, including [passages] like “This is that very one” and so on.
The *Upaniṣads* are such passages as "One should meditate upon it as the Beloved" (*priyamityetadupāsīta*);
the *Ślokas* are verses originating from the Brāhmaṇas, such as "Regarding this, there are these verses" (*tadete ślokāḥ*);
and the *Sūtras* are statements summarizing essential matters found in the Veda, such as "One should meditate [on Brahman] simply as the Self" (*ātmetyevopāsīta*).
The *anuvyākhyānas* are commentaries on the mantras;
the *vyākhyānas* are explanatory passages (*arthavādas*), or alternatively, the *anuvyākhyānas* are glosses on the summary statements of the subject matter.

Just as this remainder of the chapter [the fourth] is the explanation and commentary on the mantra "One should meditate upon [Brahman] as the Self" (*ātmety evopāsīta*), and likewise on the mantra "He who thinks 'That one is one and I am another' does not know; he is like an animal," so too [is it here].
Thus, the Brāhmaṇa is of eight kinds.
In this way, there is the inclusion of only the Mantra and Brāhmaṇa;
the manifestation of the existing Veda, which possesses a fixed arrangement, is like the breath of a person.
Nor is it preceded by human intellect or effort;
therefore, it is an independent authority regarding its own object.
Consequently, whatever has been stated therein must be accepted exactly as it is.
"By those desiring their own welfare, [it must be decided] whether it is knowledge or action.
For the determination of the modification of form depends upon the power of name and manifestation.

Indeed, when name and form—which constitute the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of the Supreme Self—are themselves being manifested, they are—in all their states—indescribable as either identical to or different from reality, like water and foam; it is these that constitute *saṃsāra*. Therefore, [the choice depends] on name...
For by that very statement, the status of the other [the world] as being merely a breath of [Brahman] is established.
Alternatively, it has been stated that the entire range of duality is the object of ignorance: “Brahman would abandon him... all this is what this Self is.
On that basis, the lack of authority (aprāmāṇya) of the Veda is suspected.
Is this stated for the purpose of removing that doubt?
[It means: "The Veda is a valid means of knowledge because it arises without effort, like the breath of a person, unlike other texts. //10//
Furthermore, it is not only during the times of its persistence and origination that the world is Brahman because of its non-existence apart from consciousness;
even at the time of dissolution,
it has no existence apart from water, just as bubbles and foam have no existence apart from water.
Thus, apart from pure consciousness (prajñāna), there is no existence for its effects—name, form, and action—as they dissolve into that very [consciousness].
Therefore, Brahman alone is to be understood as a single mass of consciousness, of one essence;
hence he says, providing an illustration to demonstrate this dissolution:
Just as the ocean is the one point of convergence for all waters,
so the skin is the one point of convergence for all tactile sensations.
In this way, the nose is the single point of convergence for all odors;
in this way, the tongue is the single point of convergence for all tastes;
in this way, the eye is the single point of convergence for all forms.
In this way, the ear is the single point of convergence for all sounds; in this way, the mind is the single point of convergence for all volitions;
in this way, the heart is the single point of convergence for all forms of knowledge.
In this way, the hands are the single path for all actions;
in this way, the genitals are the single path for all pleasures;
in this way, the anus is the single path for all excretions.
In this way, the feet are the single point of convergence for all paths;
in this way, speech is the single point of convergence for all the Vedas.
The word "sa" refers to the illustration;
"yathā" means in whatever manner [it occurs] for all waters situated in rivers, ponds, tanks, and so forth.
The ocean is the "single path" (ekāyana), meaning it is the single point of departure, the single point of dissolution, and the attainment of non-distinction;
this is the sense in which the illustration is given.
In this way, for all tactile sensations—whether soft, rough, hard, slippery, and so forth—which have wind as their essential nature, the skin is the single point of entry.
"Skin" here refers to the mere generality of touch that is the object of the skin;
all specific tactile sensations enter into it, and like rivers entering the ocean, they cease to exist apart from it.
For those were merely its configurations;
likewise, that which is denoted by the word "skin" is also a mere generality of touch within the mental construction of the mind— that is, within the mere generality of the objects of the mind—
just as specific touches are [perceived] within the object of the skin.
Having entered into that, it becomes non-existent apart from it;
likewise, the object of the mind, having entered into the mere generality that is the object of the intellect, becomes non-existent apart from it;
having become nothing but consciousness alone, it dissolves into the supreme Brahman, which is a mass of pure intelligence, like water into the ocean.

Thus, through this successive process, when sound and the rest, along with their perceiver and the instruments of perception, have dissolved into the mass of consciousness (prajñānaghana), that mass of consciousness—being free from limiting adjuncts (upādhi)—remains as Brahman: a single essence like a lump of salt, infinite, boundless, and without interval.
Therefore, one must realize that the Self alone is the one non-dual reality.
Likewise, for all odors, which are specific types of earth, the nose is the commonality of the olfactory object;
likewise, for all tastes, which are specific types of water, the eye is the commonality of the visual object;
and likewise, for sounds, the ear is the commonality of the auditory object, as previously described.
Likewise, the commonalities of the objects of the ear and other senses dissolve into the volition, which is the commonality of the object of the mind;
the commonality of the object of the mind also dissolves into the commonality of the object of the intellect, which is pure consciousness alone;
having become pure consciousness, it dissolves into the supreme mass of intelligence.

Likewise, the specific objects of the organs of action— namely speaking, grasping, moving, excreting, and sexual pleasure— are subsumed within their respective general activities and do not exist as distinct entities,
just as specific waves are subsumed within the ocean;
and those generalities are nothing but the vital breath (prāṇa) alone.
And *prāṇa* is indeed nothing but pure consciousness (*prajñāna*).
The followers of the Kauṣītaki recite: "That which is *prāṇa* is consciousness; that which is consciousness is *prāṇa*.
But is it not the case that everywhere the dissolution of only the object has been stated?
But not of the instrument;
what is the intention there? Certainly; however, the Śruti considers the instrument to be of the same genus as its object.

But it is not a different genus; rather, the sense organ is merely a particular configuration (*saṃsthānāntara*) of the object itself acting as the grasper of its own self— just as a lamp, which is a particular configuration of a specific form, is the instrument for illuminating all forms, so too the various configurations that serve as instruments are merely particular objects themselves acting as the illuminators of their own specific selves, like a lamp.

Therefore, no separate effort need be made for the dissolution of the instruments; since they consist of the same nature as their objects, their dissolution is established by the dissolution of the objects themselves. //11//
In that regard, it was proposed that "all this is what this Self is";
thereupon, the reason was stated: [because of] the commonality of being the Self and because of being born from the Self.
And there is the state of dissolution into the Self.

Therefore, because [the world] does not exist apart from consciousness at the times of its origin, subsistence, and dissolution, that which was proposed in the statements "Brahman is consciousness" and "All this is indeed the Self" has been established through reasoning.
The followers of the Purāṇas say that this [dissolution] is the natural dissolution (*svābhāvika-pralaya*).

However, that dissolution which is preceded by conscious intent, belonging to those who know Brahman and caused by the knowledge of Brahman, they call the absolute dissolution (*ātyantika*); it occurs through the cessation of ignorance (*avidyā*).
For that purpose, this specific illustration is undertaken:
Just as a lump of salt, when thrown into water, dissolves completely into the water so that it would not be possible to take it out again;
From whatever source one might take salt,
even so, my dear, this great being is infinite, boundless, and a mass of consciousness alone. Arising from these elements, it perishes after them.
"There is no consciousness after death," O Āre, I say;
thus spoke Yājñavalkya. *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 2.4.12.
In this regard, an illustration is provided by the phrase "just as that": *saindhavakhilyaḥ*. *Saindhava* is a derivative of *sindhu*;
by the word *sindhu*, water is denoted.

From the ocean (*sindhu*) comes water; that which is a modification of it, or that which exists therein, is *saindhava*. That which is both *saindhava* and a solid mass (*khilya*) is *saindhavakhilya*;
the suffix *-ya* is used in the sense of the word itself (*svārthe*), as in *khila* alone becoming *khilya*.
If it were thrown into the water, its own source, having been cast therein, it would dissolve along with the water itself;
as for that [solidity] which arises from contact with the earth and fire, it attains hardness.
Due to contact with its own source, the dissolution of that water disappears; subsequently, it is said that "the lump of salt dissolves.
This is what he means by saying, "it would dissolve following after the water itself."
Indeed, no one at all—no matter how skillful—even after extracting this remnant (*khilya*) and lifting it up as before, would be capable of grasping it.
The word *iva* is meaningless [here].
He would not be capable of grasping it; why?
From whichever place— that is, from whatever region— one might take that water and taste it,
that water would have only the taste of salt and not the state of being a solid sediment;
such is this illustration.

In this very way, O Maitreyī, this great being called the Supreme Self exists; from that great being, you— being delimited by ignorance and having entered into the state of a fragment due to connection with the limiting adjuncts of the body and organs— have become mortal, possessed of the attributes of transmigratory existence such as birth, death, hunger, thirst, and so forth, and identified with the effects of name and form, thinking, "I am the daughter of so-and-so."
That state of being a fragment of yours— produced by the delusion arising from contact with the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) consisting of the body and its organs—

has been made to enter the Great Being, its own source, the Supreme Self; which is like the great ocean, undecaying, immortal, fearless, pure, like a mass of salt water of uniform taste, a solid mass of consciousness, infinite, shoreless, without interval, and devoid of the distinctions born of the delusion produced by ignorance.

When He has entered therein, swallowed by His own source, when the state of being a fragment caused by ignorance—the state of duality—has been destroyed, there remains this one non-dual Great Being (*mahadbhūtam*). It is "Great" because it is the greatest of all, and "Being" (*bhūtam*) because it is the cause of space and the other elements;

and because its essential nature does not deviate throughout all times, it is eternally established—this is the sense of the suffix of completion (*niṣṭhā-pratyaya*) expressing its existence at all three periods of time.
Alternatively, the word *bhūta* signifies ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).
The meaning is that it is both great and ultimate (pāramārthika);
whereas although the worldly may be great, being produced by dreams or illusions, it is comparable to mountains such as the Himavat and is not an ultimate reality.
Therefore, he specifies: "But this is both great and unprecedented.

It is "infinite" (ananta) because no end to it is found; lest it be thought that this might be merely relative, he specifies further: "without limit" (apāra). "Representation" (vijñapti) is consciousness (vijñāna).
It is called a "mass of consciousness" (*vijñānaghana*) because it is both consciousness and a mass;
the word "mass" (*ghana*) is intended to exclude any other distinct category, just as one speaks of a "gold-mass" (*suvarṇaghana*) or an "iron-mass" (*ayoghana*).
The word "only" (*eva*) has the sense of restriction, meaning that no other distinct category exists in the interval.

If this one non-dual reality is, from the perspective of ultimate truth, pure and untouched by the sufferings of saṃsāra, then what is the cause of this fragmentary state of the Self that has arisen—characterized by birth, death, happiness, suffering, "I," "mine," and so forth—and which is afflicted by the manifold phenomena of saṃsāra?

To this it is said: From these elements—which have transformed into the forms of effects, instruments, and objects, consisting of name and form, and resembling foam and bubbles upon the pure water-like Supreme Self—[this state arises].
For those whose limits are the objects of the senses, there is a dissolution within Brahman— the mass of pure consciousness— by means of the knowledge of ultimate discrimination,

like a river [into the ocean]; having arisen from these elements which are the causes and are denoted by the word "truth," just as a reflection of the sun, moon, and so forth arises from water, like a lump of salt.

Or, just as a clear crystal assumes the state of redness and so forth due to limiting adjuncts such as lac-dye, even so, through the limiting adjuncts of the elements that constitute the body and the organs, it arises— having arisen properly— as a fragment of the specific self (*viśeṣātma-khilya*).

From whichever elements it has arisen, those very elements, when transformed into the forms of the body, the organs, and sense-objects, become the causes for that fragment of the specific self of the Self.
Through the instruction of the scriptures and the teacher, the distinctions [of the individual self] are dissolved and perish in the knowledge of Brahman, like rivers in the ocean.
As they perish—just as foam, bubbles, and the like vanish in water—this very state of being a distinct, limited individual (*viśeṣātmakhilyabhāva*) perishes.
It is just as the reflection of the moon, a crystal, and so forth vanishes when the causes for its appearance, such as water or a mirror, are removed.

Just as the true nature of the moon and other such objects remains established in ultimate reality, so too does the mass of consciousness—endless, boundless, and pure—remain established. In that state, for one who is liberated from the aggregate of the body and its organs, there is no longer any perception of particularity after death; thus it is, O Maitreyī.

I say that there is no notion of distinction— such as "I am this person," "I am his son," "this is my field," "this is my wealth," "I am happy," "I am miserable," and so forth— because such a notion is produced by ignorance (avidyā).

Since ignorance has been utterly destroyed by the knowledge of Brahman (brahmavidyā), how could a notion of distinction possibly arise for the knower of Brahman, who abides in the nature of pure consciousness?

"Even for one abiding in a body, a specific designation is not possible, much less for one who is entirely liberated from the body and the senses"—thus, it is said, Yājñavalkya spoke this supreme vision of ultimate reality to his wife Maitreyī. 12.
Thus enlightened,
Maitreyī said: "Right here, sir, you have bewildered me by saying that after death there is no consciousness."
He said: "Indeed, I do not speak in delusion; this is sufficient for understanding. Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.13.

She, it is said, spoke thus to Maitreyī: "Right here, with respect to this very same single reality that is Brahman, my Lord has caused me confusion by describing it as possessing contradictory attributes.
She says: "In this very matter, my Lord, the venerable one has bewildered me; he has created confusion. How so?

By first asserting, 'It is indeed a mass of consciousness,' and then later stating, 'After departing, it does not have any cognition. Thus it is said that he described it as possessing contradictory attributes.
How is it that there is "nothing but a mass of consciousness"?
Or how is it that "there is no perception after death"?
For fire is not simultaneously both hot and cold.
"Therefore, I am deluded in this matter.
Yājñavalkya said: "Indeed, Maitreyī, I do not speak out of delusion; the meaning is that I do not utter a delusive statement. [Maitreyī asked:
"But how did you speak of contradictory attributes—being a mass of consciousness (*vijñānaghana*) and yet being the absence of perception (*saṃjñābhāva*)?"
I have not stated this with the intention that it be understood as one [identical] thing;
rather, it is you who, through delusion, have grasped this as a single entity possessing contradictory properties,
whereas I have not said so.
But this has been stated by me: that state of fragmentation (*khilyabhāva*) of the Self, which is brought about by ignorance (*avidyā*) and consists in its connection with the body and the organs;

when that [state] is destroyed by knowledge (*vidyā*), there follows the specific notion (*viśeṣasaṃjñā*) caused by it, characterized by the perception of difference, which relates to the body and so forth.

When the limiting adjunct (upādhi) consisting of the aggregate of the body and its organs has been dissolved, that [reflection] perishes due to the absence of its cause, just as the reflection of the moon and so forth perishes upon the destruction of its substratum such as water; and likewise, the light and other qualities caused by it perish.

However, there is no destruction of the nature of the non-transmigrating Brahman, which is a mass of consciousness (vijñānaghana), any more than there is destruction of the true nature of the ultimate sun or moon; for it has been stated that "it is a mass of consciousness."
That Self is the soul of the entire world;
from the perspective of ultimate reality, it is not subject to destruction because there is no destruction of what is truly existent.
However, the state of being a fragmented, limited entity is perishable and is produced by ignorance.
This is because of another scriptural passage: "Modification is a mere verbal handle, a name" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.1.4).
But this [Self] is the ultimate reality: "Verily, this Self is indestructible, O Maitreyī."
Therefore, indeed, enough! This great being, infinite and boundless, which has been described for the sake of understanding—to know it is sufficient.
For where there is, as it were, duality, there one smells another, there one sees another. But [where there is no duality],... Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.14.
One hears another; one smells another; one speaks to another; one thinks of another; one perceives another.
But where for him everything has become the Self alone—then by what and whom should one smell? Then by what and whom should one smell? Then by what and whom [should one speak]?
What would one see, and by what? What would one hear, and by what? What would one speak to, and by what? What would one think, and by what? What would one perceive, and by what?
By what could one perceive that by which one perceives all this?
O Maitreyī, by what could one perceive the perceiver? Thus spoke Yājñavalkya.
How, then, is it said that "after death there is no consciousness"?
Listen:
in that state where, within the limited self produced by the adjuncts of the aggregate of effects and instruments imagined through ignorance, there exists a fragmentary condition—
For indeed, although non-duality is the ultimate reality, within that non-dual Brahman, duality—as if distinct, as if another entity separate from the Self—is perceived.
Now, one might argue that because duality is compared to non-duality, it must therefore be ultimately real. This is not so;
for there are other scriptural passages such as, "Modification is a mere verbal handle, a name," and "One alone without a second; this all is the Self."

In that regard, because there is, as it were, duality, therefore this other Self—the one that has become a fragment of the Supreme Self—is not the ultimate reality; it is like the reflection of the moon in water. Being "other," it smells the "other" object of smell by means of the "other" sense of smell.
The expression "the other [smells] the other" is intended to demonstrate the grammatical factors (kārakas), while "it smells" denotes both the action and its result.

Just as when one says "he cuts," both the act of striking down repeatedly and the resulting state of being split into two parts are denoted by the single word "cuts," because [the action] culminates in the result and no result is perceived apart from the action;
so too, the other [sense] smells one thing with another sense— the olfactory organ— and likewise cognizes everything as previously described.
This is the state of one possessed by ignorance (*avidyā*).
But where ignorance has been brought to destruction by the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*), there is the non-existence of anything other than the Self.

Or rather, for this knower of Brahman, everything—name, form, and so forth—has been dissolved into the Self alone, and the Self alone has come to be. Wherein the Self alone has thus become [all], by what instrument could one smell what, and who [could smell it]?
One should smell and likewise see, and thus one should understand;
for in all cases, an action is accomplished by means of its factors (kāraka).
Therefore, in the absence of the factors, the action is impossible, and in the absence of the action, there is an absence of the result.
Therefore, it is only while ignorance exists that the conventional dealings of action, agent, and fruit occur, not for the knower of Brahman.
Because everything is indeed the Self, there exists no agent, nor action, nor fruit apart from the Self. Furthermore, nothing that is non-Self can ever become the Self for anyone.
Therefore, it is by ignorance alone that non-selfhood is imagined; in ultimate reality, there is nothing whatsoever apart from the Self.
Consequently, when there is the realization of the oneness of the ultimate Self, the notions of action, agent, and fruit are untenable.
Thus, due to this contradiction, for the knower of Brahman, there is an absolute cessation of actions and their means.
The statement "By what? What? is intended as a challenge and to demonstrate the impossibility of any other mode [of existence].
This is because, in any manner whatsoever, the causal factors such as the action, the instrument, and so forth, are untenable.
The meaning is that nothing could ever live by anything, in any way, or in any manner.

Even in that state of ignorance where one perceives another, by what could one perceive that by which all this is known? For that instrument by which one knows is already engaged with the object to be known; and indeed, the desire to know belongs to the knower only with respect to the object to be known, not with respect to the Self.
Furthermore, the Self is not an object for the Self, as fire is not its own object; and for a knower, knowledge is not possible regarding that which is not an object.
Therefore, by what instrument could one know that Knower by whom all this is known? Or who else could know that Knower?
But when, for the knower of Brahman who has discerned the ultimate reality, there remains only the Knower alone, non-dual, then—O Maitreyī—by what could one know that Knower? Thus it is said. //4//
Thus ends the fourth Brāhmaṇa of the second Adhyāya in the Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya.
The Maitreyī-brāhmaṇa is commenced with the intention that that which is the exclusive means for attaining immortality, independent of ritual action, must be declared;
and that is the knowledge of the Self, characterized by the requirement of the renunciation of all things.
When the Self is known, all this becomes known;
and the Self is dearer than everything else.
Therefore, it has been said that the Self must be seen, and the methods for seeing it have been stated as: "It is to be heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon."
In this regard, it is to be heard from the teacher and the scriptures;
it is to be reflected upon through reasoning.

And as for that reasoning, it has been stated [as follows]: regarding the proposition "all this is indeed the Self," the statement of the reason consists in the fact that there is a single commonality with the Self, a single origin from the Self, and a single dissolution into the Self.

In this regard, the reason [for the world's unity] is suspected to be unestablished; therefore, to remove that suspicion regarding the origin and dissolution known as the single universal Self (ātmaikasāmānya), this Brāhmaṇa is commenced.
For the entire world, beginning with the earth, exists in a state of mutual assistance between benefactor and beneficiary.

And whatever in the world exists in a state of mutual benefit between cause and effect is seen to be preceded by a single cause, to consist of a single universal essence, and to undergo a single dissolution.
Therefore, this world, characterized by earth and the other elements, must likewise exist as such because of its mutual relationship of helper and helped;
for this is the meaning revealed in this Brāhmaṇa.
Alternatively, it establishes that the Self alone is the origin, maintenance, and dissolution of all this, as was previously asserted in the proposition "the Self alone is all this."

For instance, it has been stated by the Naiyāyikas that the conclusion (nigamana) is the restatement of the proposition (pratijñā) following the presentation of the reason (hetu). Others have explained that, up to the illustration of the drum, there is the scriptural statement for the purpose of hearing; prior to the Madhu-brāhmaṇa, there is the instruction for reflection (mantavya) by means of demonstrating logical justification; and by the Madhu-brāhmaṇa, however, the injunction for meditative contemplation (nididhyāsana) is expressed.
In every respect, however, one must reflect upon that very thing which has been determined through scripture by means of reasoning;

and just as one reflects upon what has been understood through reasoning and ascertained through both reasoning and scripture, so too is meditative contemplation (*nididhyāsana*) performed. Thus, a separate injunction for meditative contemplation is indeed purposeless. Therefore, it is our view that the division into separate sections for hearing (*śravaṇa*), reflection (*manana*), and meditative contemplation (*nididhyāsana*) is purposeless.
In every respect, however, the meaning of the two preceding chapters is summarized in this Brāhmaṇa:
"This earth is honey for all beings;
all beings are honey for this earth."

This person consisting of light and consisting of immortality who is in this earth, and this person consisting of light and consisting of immortality who is here in the body with respect to the self—he is indeed this Self.
This is the immortal; this is Brahman; this is all.

This earth is honey for all beings; it is honey for all beings, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, meaning it is their effect, "honey" because it is like honey— just as a single honey-cake is produced by many bees, so too this earth is produced by all beings.
In the same way, all beings are honey for this earth;

and furthermore, that person who exists in this earth, consisting of splendor, consisting of light alone, consisting of immortality, and characterized by immortality, and that person who exists within the body (the *adhyātma*), being corporeal (*śārīra*), consisting of splendor and consisting of immortality, as previously described.
And he, identifying with the subtle body (liṅga),
is honey by virtue of performing benefit for all beings,
and all beings are honey for him.
By the force of the word "and" (ca), this fourfold group is thus one effect of all the elements, and all the elements are its effects; therefore, it has a single cause preceding it.

Since this was born from a single cause, that alone is the one Brahman in the ultimate sense, while everything else is an effect—a modification consisting merely of a name and a verbal handle. Such is the meaning of all these honey-chapter passages.
In brief:
this very thing is that which was promised, namely, "All this is what this Self is.
This is the immortal; that knowledge of the Self which was stated as the means to immortality for Maitreyī—this is that immortal.

"This is Brahman"—that which I shall speak to you and cause you to know, which was introduced at the beginning of the chapter, and the knowledge of whose subject matter is called "the knowledge of Brahman" (brahmavidyā)—is this entire [reality], because through the realization of this Brahman, everything becomes [known]. //1//
These waters are honey for all beings;
all beings are honey for these waters.

And this person consisting of light and consisting of immortality who is in these waters, and this person consisting of light and consisting of immortality who is with respect to the self (adhyātma) in semen—he is this very Self.
This is the immortal; this is Brahman; this is all.
Likewise, [the presence of] water;
specifically, within the semen, there is the particular abiding of water in the internal self. //2//
This fire is honey for all beings;
all beings are honey for this fire.

This person consisting of splendor and consisting of immortality who is in this fire, and this person consisting of speech, consisting of splendor, and consisting of immortality who is with respect to the self—this very one is that Self.
This is the immortal; this is Brahman; this is all.
Likewise, fire [is present]; specifically, fire is situated there. //3//
This wind, indeed, is honey for all beings;
all beings are honey for this wind.

This person consisting of light and consisting of immortality who is in this wind, and this person consisting of light and consisting of immortality who is the vital breath (prāṇa) with respect to the self— he who is this Self,
he is this immortal, he is Brahman, he is all this.

Likewise is the air. Internally, it is the vital breath (*prāṇa*); it possesses the nature of honey because it assists living beings by initiating their bodies. It also possesses the nature of honey because it assists the elements contained within it, such as those consisting of light, by serving as their instruments.
And so it has been said: "Of that very speech, the earth is the body, and this fire is its form consisting of light. (4)
This sun is honey for all beings;
all beings are honey for this sun.

This person consisting of splendor and consisting of immortality who is in this sun, and this person consisting of splendor and consisting of immortality who is in the self with respect to the eye—he is indeed this Self.
This is the immortal; this is Brahman; this is all.
Likewise, the sun is honey; that which pertains to the eye is honey with respect to the self. //5//
These quarters are honey for all beings;
and all beings are honey for these quarters.

And this person consisting of light and consisting of immortality who is in these quarters, and this person consisting of light and consisting of immortality who is within the self—the one heard through the ear—he is indeed this Self;
he is this Immortal, he is Brahman, he is all this.
Likewise, the quarters are honey.

Although the ear belongs to the quarters, it is especially present within during the moment of hearing a sound; thus, it is "internal" (*adhyātma*). That which exists in an echo (*pratiśrutkā*) at the time of hearing is "pertaining to the echo" (*prātiśrutka*). //6//
This moon is honey for all beings;
all beings are honey for this moon.

And this person consisting of light and consisting of nectar who is in this moon, and this person consisting of light and consisting of nectar who is the mental self (mānasa) within the body—this very one is that which is the Self; this is the immortal, this is Brahman, this is all.
Likewise, the moon is the mental [element] within. //7//
This lightning is honey for all beings;
all beings are honey for this lightning.

This person consisting of light and consisting of immortality who is in this lightning, and this person consisting of light and consisting of immortality who is with respect to the self (adhyātma) as the luminous one—this very one is that Self.
This is the immortal; this is Brahman; this is all.
Likewise, lightning;
that which exists in the bodily heat of the skin is the taijasa [element] internally. //8//
This thunder is honey for all beings;
all beings are honey for this thunder.

And this person consisting of splendor, consisting of immortality, who is in this thundering cloud, and this person consisting of splendor, consisting of immortality, who is the one relating to sound within the self (adhyātma)—he is indeed this very Self;
he is this immortality, he is Brahman, he is all this.
Likewise, there is the *stanayitnu* (thunder).

Although the *śābda* (pertaining to sound) exists internally within sound, it nonetheless occurs specifically with respect to the tone (*svara*); thus, it is the *sauvara* (pertaining to tone) that is internal. //9//
This space is honey for all beings;
all beings are honey for this space.

This person consisting of light and consisting of immortality who is in this space, and this person consisting of light and consisting of immortality who is within the self in the space of the heart—this very one is that Self.
This is the immortal; this is Brahman; this is all.
Likewise is space; for here, within, is the internal space. //10//
This dharma is honey for all beings;
all beings are honey for this dharma.

This person consisting of splendor and consisting of immortality who is in this dharma, and this person consisting of splendor and consisting of immortality who is the internal dharma—this very one is that which is the Self;
this is the immortal, this is Brahman, this is all.
Although this *dharma* is not directly perceptible, it is designated as "this is *dharma*" by means of its perceptible effect produced by it, just as if it were perceptible.

Furthermore, *dharma* has been explained as characterized by the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*; it is the restrainer even of the Kṣatriyas and others, the cause of the diversity of the world because it is the cause of the transformation of the earth and other elements, and it takes the form of being practiced by living beings.
By means of that [practice], there is the designation "this is *dharma*" based on direct perception.
In this context, truth (*satya*) and Dharma have been taught as non-different, characterized respectively by the scriptures and right conduct;
however, they are designated here as distinct even though they are one,
because they initiate action in the form of a distinction between the visible and the invisible.

That dharma which is unseen and called *apūrva* initiates its effect through an unseen form consisting of both the universal and the particular: by its universal aspect, it becomes the impeller of the earth and other elements; and by its particular aspect, [it is the impeller] of the aggregate of effects and instruments within the self (*adhyātma*). In this regard, that which exists in this dharma—the impeller of the earth and so forth—is "consisting of light" (*tejomaya*); likewise, that which exists in the dharma which produces the aggregate of effects and instruments within the self is "pertaining to dharma" (*dhārma*). (11)
This truth is honey for all beings;
all beings are honey for this truth.
And this radiant, immortal person who is in this truth, and this radiant, immortal person who is within the self (adhyātma), namely Sātya—this very one is that Self.
This is the immortal; this is Brahman; this is all.
Likewise, that which is practiced as seen in the form of conduct is called "truth" (satya), and that itself is Dharma. That too is of two kinds, by way of its nature as both general and particular.
The general form resides in [the elements] such as earth, while the particular form resides in the aggregate of the body and its organs.

Among these, "truth" (satya) exists in the truth that consists of present activity residing in earth and the other elements, and likewise in the truth residing within the individual in the aggregate of the body and its organs. Thus, that which exists [in these] is "truth."
For it is stated in another scriptural passage: "By truth the wind blows. (12)
This human [world] is honey for all beings;
all beings are honey for this human [world].

This person consisting of splendor and consisting of immortality who is here in this human [body], and this person consisting of splendor and consisting of immortality with respect to the self (adhyātma)—he is indeed this Self.
This is the immortal; this is Brahman; this is all.
This specific aggregate of causes and effects is impelled by both *dharma* and *adharma*.
That particular class of birth (*jāti-viśeṣa*) with which it becomes associated is such as that of humans and so forth.
In this regard, all classes of living beings distinguished by such births as human and so on are seen to exist in a state of mutual assistance and dependence.
Therefore, even the human species and so forth are honey for all beings;
therein, the human species and so forth are designated in two ways: as both external and internal. //13//
This Self is honey for all beings;
all beings are honey for this Self.
And this person consisting of light and consisting of immortality who is in this self, and this self consisting of light and consisting of immortality—this very one is that which is this self;
this is the immortal, this is Brahman, this is all.
But that which is the aggregate of causes and effects, distinguished by the human and other species—that very Self is the honey of all beings.
Now, one might object: "Is this not already indicated by the term *śārīra* (the embodied) in the section concerning the earth? No; for in that instance, only the earthly element was intended.

But this, which is the Self of all—wherein all distinctions such as the internal (adhyātma) and the elemental (adhibhūta) have subsided, and which is distinguished by the hosts of deities of all beings—is called "this very Self," namely the aggregate of causes and effects.
Within this Self, this person (puruṣa), consisting of light, consisting of immortality, the unembodied essence, and the Self of all, is pointed out.
However, because it has been pointed out in part within the earth and other elements, it is not pointed out here [as a whole], due to the absence of internal distinctions.
But that which remains, consisting of consciousness, for whose sake this aggregate of the body and the subtle body exists as the self—that is what is called "this self. //14//
This very Self is the overlord of all, the king of all beings. Just as all the spokes are fixed in the nave and the felly of a chariot wheel, so [are all things fixed in this Self].
In the very same way, within this Self all beings, all gods, all worlds, all vital breaths, and all these selves are contained.

When this self consisting of consciousness—which was previously remaining [as a limited entity]—is introduced into that Self which is the ultimate reality through the knowledge of Brahman, being distinguished from the adjuncts of the aggregate of effects and instruments produced by ignorance, it becomes thus described:
without interior, without exterior, made whole, become a single mass of pure intelligence; this is the Self of all beings.
He is to be honored by all, the sovereign lord of all beings, independent of all beings— not like a prince or a minister— but rather the king of all beings;
the term "sovereign lord" (adhipati) serves as a specific qualification of his kingship.
There may be someone who, by adopting conduct befitting a king, is a king but not a sovereign; therefore, he specifies "sovereign" (*adhipati*).
Thus, the wise man who knows the Self as the Self of all beings becomes liberated—that is, he who knows Brahman.
This explains what was stated [in the scripture]: "Men think that by the knowledge of Brahman they will become everything; what then is that Brahman, by knowing which one becomes all?
Having heard from both the teacher and the sacred tradition that the Self alone is indeed the Self of all in this manner, [one realizes it].

Having reflected and understood through reasoning—just as it has been directly shown in the Madhu Brāhmaṇa—from that very knowledge of Brahman characterized in this way, [it was seen that] even previously one was indeed Brahman, yet through ignorance one was non-Brahman;

and though being everything, one was non-everything. Having cast aside that ignorance by means of this knowledge, the knower of Brahman, being Brahman itself, became Brahman; he, being everything, became everything.
The purpose for which this treatise was commenced has been fully accomplished:
namely, that the entire universe is established within this Knower of Brahman, who is the Self of all and the Universal Self.
To illustrate this point, an analogy is provided: "Just as all the spokes are fixed upon the nave and the rim of a chariot wheel"—this is a well-known fact.
In this very same way, within this Self which has become the Supreme Self for the knower of Brahman, there are all beings from Brahmā down to a tuft of grass,
all the gods beginning with Agni, and all the worlds beginning with Bhūr.
All vital breaths, beginning with speech,
are all these selves that enter into each body like the moon reflected in water; they are fashioned by ignorance,
and the entire world is offered up within this [Self].
That which was stated regarding what the knower of Brahman, Vāmadeva, realized— "I became Manu and Sūrya"—
that state of being the Self of all has been explained.
That very knower, the knower of Brahman, possessing all adjuncts and being the Self of all, becomes everything.

It is without attributes, beyond description, without interior or exterior, a single mass of consciousness, undecaying, immortal, fearless, immovable, and characterized by "not this, not this," being neither gross nor subtle.

Not knowing this reality, certain logicians and those who consider themselves learned among the knowers of scripture—imagining it to be contrary to the meaning of the sacred texts—fall into profound delusion through their conceptualizations.
This very same reality is declared in these two verses of the *Mantras*: "The one that is unmoving, swifter than the mind," and "It moves, and it moves not."
And likewise in the Taittirīyaka: "There is nothing higher than which there is no other," "He sits singing this Sāman," and "I am food, I am food, I am food," and so forth.
And likewise in the Chāndogya: "Eating, playing, and rejoicing," "If he is desirous of the world of the fathers," and "Possessing all fragrances, possessing all tastes," and so forth.
And in the Ātharvaṇa: "The all-knowing, the all-wise," and "Farther than the far, yet here near at hand."
“In the *Kaṭhavallīs* as well: ‘Smaller than the small, greater than the great’; ‘Who [knows] that God, the intoxication and non-intoxication’; and ‘Standing, He transcends all other moving things.

Likewise, in the *Gītās*: ‘I am the sacrifice, I am the oblation’; ‘I am the father of this world’; ‘He takes no one’s sin’; ‘The same in all beings’; ‘Immersed in the undifferentiated among the differentiated’; ‘Devouring and procreating’—thus, the meaning of such scriptures appears to be contradictory.”
Considering what appears [to them] as real and conceptualizing it for the sake of determining the nature of objects—

conceptualizing such things as "the self exists," "the self does not exist," "there is an agent," "there is no agent," "one is liberated," "one is bound," "everything is momentary," "it is mere consciousness," or "it is empty"— they do not reach the further shore of ignorance,
because they perceive contradictory properties in all things.
Therefore, in this regard, only those who follow the path shown by the scriptures and the teacher reach the further shore of ignorance;
only they shall cross over this bottomless ocean of delusion.
Not others who follow their own cleverness. //15//

The sacred knowledge of Brahman, which is the means for attaining immortality and about which Maitreyī had asked her husband— "Tell me that alone, O Venerable One, which you know to be the means for immortality"— has now been completed.
This narrative is for the purpose of praising this knowledge of Brahman; these two verses serve to briefly illuminate its meaning.

For, by being thus praised through both the Mantras and the Brāhmaṇa, the fact that the knowledge of Brahman is the means for attaining immortality and all things is made manifest and brought onto the royal road—just as the rising sun dispels the dense darkness.

Moreover, thus praised, this knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*), protected by Indra, is difficult to attain even for the gods. Therefore, the two physicians of the gods, Aśvinī, obtained this Indra-protected knowledge only with great effort. Having cut off the head of a Brāhmaṇa and joined the head of a horse to him, and when that [horse-head] was cut off by Indra, they again joined his own original head to him; and by means of that very head of the Brāhmaṇa, the remainder of the instruction was completed.
The knowledge of Brahman has been heard;
therefore, there has never been, nor will there ever be, anything superior to that as a means for achieving the goal of man, much less anything existing in the present.
Thus, there is no praise higher than this.
Moreover, it is praised in this way: "In the world, it is well known that action (*karman*) is the means for achieving all human goals (*puruṣārtha*);
and that action is accomplished through wealth (*vitta*)."
Therefore, there is no hope for immortality [through ritual action].
This very immortality is attained through the knowledge of the Self alone, independent of ritual action;
for although it was mentioned in the section on ritual action, it is [discussed] here in the section concerning the absolute [knowledge].
Having transcended the section on action because of its opposition to it, [this knowledge] is declared, together with absolute renunciation, as the means for attaining immortality.
Therefore, there is no other means for achieving the goal of man superior to this.

Furthermore, the knowledge of Brahman is thus praised, for the entire world delights in dualities, according to the Vedic text: "He indeed found no delight; therefore, one does not delight being alone."

Although Yājñavalkya was common to the world, by the power of his knowledge of the Self, he abandoned attachment to worldly life—consisting of wife, children, wealth, and so forth—and became one satisfied in wisdom and delighting in the Self. Moreover, the knowledge of Brahman is thus praised because it was imparted by Yājñavalkya, even as he was departing from the path of worldly existence, solely for the sake of his beloved wife, as indicated by the words: "I am speaking what is dear to you; come, sit here."
In this regard, we have stated that this is a narrative intended for the purpose of praise.
What, then, is that narrative? It is said:
"This indeed is that honey which Dadhyañc Ātharvaṇa spoke to the Aśvins."

Seeing this, the seer said: "O heroes, I make manifest that powerful deed of yours for the sake of gain, like thunder making rain manifest, since Dadhyañc Ātharvaṇa, with the head of a horse, proclaimed to you the honeyed secret. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.5.16)
The word "this" (idam) refers to that which was just mentioned,
because it is present in the mind;
the particle "vai" is used for the purpose of recollection.

The word "tat" (that) refers back to what was previously mentioned in another context within the narrative; by means of the particle "vai," it recalls that which was indicated in the section on the Pravargya rite but not yet revealed as the "madhu" (honey).
It designates this here [as follows]: "That honey which was indicated in the section on the Pravargya..."
This very honey has been indicated here immediately following [the previous section] by the passage beginning with, "This earth...
How was it suggested at the end of that context? [It says: "Dadhyañ Ātharvaṇa indeed taught these two the Brāhmaṇa named Madhu.
That is their beloved abode; through this, he approaches that very [abode] for them."
He said, "Indra has indeed seized me; if you were to teach this to anyone else, he would cut off your head from that very spot.
Therefore, I am afraid that he might cut off my head; however, I shall initiate you both."
The two said, "We shall protect you from that. He asked, "How will you protect me?
They replied, "When they lead you away, we shall cut off your head, carry it elsewhere, and set it down."
"Then, having brought the horse's head, we shall replace it for you; with that, you will recite the Veda to us. When you no longer recite it,"
"Then Indra will cut off that head of yours;
then we two shall bring back your own head and replace it for you.
"So be it," he said, and he initiated them both.
When they brought those two [heads], they then cut off his head and set them aside; then,
having brought the horse's head, they replaced it upon him.
Therefore, he taught it to both of them.
When he had taught it to both of them, Indra then cut off his head.
Then, having brought back his own head, they two restored it to him.
However, only that honey which constitutes a constituent part of the Pravargya rite was mentioned there,
and not the "chest" (kakṣya) known as the knowledge of the Self.
The narrative recounted therein is presented here for the purpose of praise.
This indeed is that honey which Dadhyañc Ātharvaṇa taught to the two Aśvins through this elaboration. Regarding this, the seer [says]: "This is the ritual action;
the seer is the mantra."
Seeing and perceiving, he said: "He has risen. How so? The connection is with the word "taddarśaḥ" (the sight of that), which is separated [in the text].
*Daṃsaḥ* is a name for an action; and what kind of action is that *daṃsaḥ*? It is fierce (*ugra*), meaning cruel.
"Vām" means "of you two. O "narā," O Aśvins who have the form of men! And for what purpose was that deed performed?
For the sake of gain;
for even in the world, one who is greedy for profit performs cruel deeds, and these two are observed in exactly the same way as that person in the world.
Then I shall make manifest—that is, I shall reveal—whatever has been done by you two in secret. What is it like?
It is said: "Like the thundering of Parjanya. The particle *na* is used here in the Veda in the sense of a comparison, as an honorific placed after the word.
It does not have the sense of negation;
it is like "na aśvam," meaning "like a horse. Just as in that case.
The connection is as follows: "Just as Parjanya, like a thunderer, makes his rain manifest through sounds such as thundering, so do I make manifest the cruel deed of you two.
Now, one might object: how can these two mantras be for the purpose of praising the Aśvins, since they contain words of censure?
This is not a fault;
this is merely praise, not words of censure.
"Since not even a single hair of yours is diminished while you perform such an exceedingly cruel deed,
and nothing else whatsoever is lost,
these two [verses] are for the purpose of praise."
For worldly people remember both censure and praise;
likewise, in the world, censure is well known to take the form of praise.
[There was] one named Dadhyañc, a descendant of Atharvan.
The particle *ha* is an expletive.
That which Madhuka Ātharvaṇa, through his two yoked ones, spoke with the head—the head—of the horse, that is, the honey characterized by self-knowledge;
*īm* is an expletive particle. //16//
This indeed is that honey which Dadhyañc Ātharvaṇa spoke to the Aśvins.
Seeing this, a seer declared: "O Aśvins, you restored the horse's head to Dadhyañc Ātharvaṇa."
"This indeed is that honey," and so forth, is for the purpose of showing another mantra as before;
likewise, another mantra follows that very narrative:
[there was] an Atharvaṇa named Dadhyañc.
Since another [teacher] named Ātharvaṇa exists, [the text] specifies: "Dadhyañc by name, the son of Atharvan.

To that Dadhyañc, the son of Atharvan, [he spoke] the words of the seer of the mantra: "O Aśvins," [referring to] the horse's head (*aśvyam*), which is the head belonging to the horse (*aśvasya svabhūtam*).
When the head of the Brahmin had been cut off, you two, having performed such an exceedingly cruel deed as cutting off the horse's head, sent that horse-head toward the Brahmin.

And that Atharvan spoke to you both that honey which he had previously promised, saying, "I shall tell it. For what purpose did he speak thus, having entered into a state where his life was in jeopardy? This is explained as follows:
Desiring to fulfill that which was previously promised as true, he says this:
for the preservation of truth and dharma is weightier even than life; this is the indication of that.
What honey did he proclaim?
It is called *tvāṣṭra* because it belongs to Tvaṣṭṛ; Tvaṣṭṛ is Āditya,
and when the head of the sacrifice was cut off, it became Tvaṣṭṛ.
The *pravargya* rite is for the purpose of reconnecting that [head].

In this context, the knowledge that constitutes a constituent part of the *pravargya* rite is the vision concerning the severing and rejoining of the head of the sacrifice, which is the "Madhu of Tvaṣṭṛ.
O *dastra*, *dastrau*—you two who are the destroyers (*upakṣapayitārau*) of the forces of others, or of enemies.
O destroyers of enemies!
Furthermore, it was not only the honey related to the ritual action concerning Tvaṣṭṛ that was spoken of by you both;
rather, there is also that secret, hidden knowledge concerning the Supreme Self—which is "honey" as described in the Madhu-brāhmaṇa and revealed in the two preceding chapters.
And "he shall proclaim that to you two" is understood to follow [from the previous verse]. //17//
This indeed is that honey which Dadhyañc Ātharvaṇa spoke to the two Aśvins.
Seeing this, a seer declared: "He made bodies with two feet; He made bodies with four feet."
"Having first become a bird, he entered the city as a person.
Indeed, this person dwells within all cities;
there is nothing whatsoever that is not covered by him.
Thereby, nothing at all remains uncovered.
"This indeed is that honey," as before.
These two mantras at the end serve to conclude the narrative related to the Pravargya rite.
The meaning of the two chapters concerning the purpose of the Pravargya ritual has been elucidated by these two mantras in the form of a narrative.
The meaning of these two chapters, concerning the knowledge of Brahman and its goal, must be elucidated by the following two verses;
therefore, the next section proceeds.
It begins with the words: "That which is the secret enclosure, O Atharvan, you who have uttered the honeyed [hymns] for the two of you."
What, then, is this honey? It is said:

"He made cities before. That Supreme Lord, who performs the process of the manifestation of the unmanifest Name-and-Form (*nāmarūpa*), having first created the worlds beginning with Bhūḥ, made—i.e., fashioned—the two-footed bodies.

Bodies characterized by two feet are human bodies; bird-bodies [are those] before you. Bodies characterized by four feet are the bodies of animals. The Śruti explains the meaning of the statement "that Lord, having become a bird—the subtle body—entered the bodies before"—namely: "This very Puruṣa [is present] in all years, in all bodies."
Because he lies within the city (*puri*), being thus situated within the city, he is called the Person (*puruṣa*).
By him nothing at all is uncovered—that is, nothing whatsoever is unshielded or unshrouded.
Likewise, by him nothing at all is unenclosed—nothing has not been entered within by what is external or internal; there is nothing that is not covered.
Thus, that very Self, by way of name and manifestation, exists internally and externally in the form of the body and the instruments [of action].
The meaning is that the mantra beginning with "He made the cities" (puraścakre) briefly teaches the oneness of the Self. //18//

This indeed is that honey which Dadhyañc Ātharvaṇa spoke to the two Aśvins. Seeing this, a seer declared: "In form after form he became a counterpart; that was his form for the purpose of being seen."
"Indra moves in many forms through his powers of illusion (māyā), for his bay horses are yoked—ten hundred and ten.
Indeed, this [Self] is the bay horses; this is the ten, the thousands, the many, and the infinite.
This very Brahman is without before, without after, without within, and without without.
"This Self is Brahman, the perceiver of all"—this is the instruction. (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.5.19)
"This indeed is that honey," and so forth, as before.
"He became the counterpart (pratirūpa) of every form" means he became another form.
A counterpart, or rather a conformable one (anurūpa), is born: whatever the configuration of the parents who procreated him, a son of that very configuration and conforming to them is born.
For indeed, a four-footed creature is not born from a two-footed one, nor is a two-footed one born from a four-footed one.
It is that very Supreme Lord who, manifesting name and form, became a counterpart to every form.
But for what purpose did he come to be a counterpart?
Thus it is said: that [differentiation] is for the sake of making known, for the sake of manifesting, the form of this Self.
For if name and form were not differentiated, then the unconditioned form of this Self, called the "mass of consciousness," would not be made known.
But when name and form become differentiated through the manifestation of effects and instruments, then its form would be perceived.
Indra— the Supreme Lord— by means of *māyās*, that is, by means of his powers of wisdom (*prajñā*), or rather, by means of false identifications produced from name and form.

But not in the ultimate sense; he is perceived or understood as having many forms and manifold shapes, while in reality he is of a single form, being a mass of pure consciousness through the various cognitions of ignorance.
For what reason?

Because, like a chariot-horseman who has harnessed his horses, he [drives them] for the sake of illuminating his own objects; for "his bay steeds" (*harayaḥ*) are so called because of their seizing (*haraṇa*), that is, the sense-faculties (*indriyāṇi*).
"Hundreds and tens" means that because there is a great plurality of types of living beings, there are hundreds and tens;

therefore, due to the plurality of sense faculties and their objects, these [scriptures] were composed for the purpose of illuminating those [faculties and objects], not for the purpose of illuminating a self.
For it is said in the *Kaṭha Upaniṣad*: "The Self-existent pierced the openings outward.
Therefore, [the Self] is perceived through those very forms of objects, and not by way of its own nature as a single-flavored mass of consciousness (*prajñānaghana*).

If this were so, then it would follow that this Supreme Lord is one thing and the *hari*s (senses) are another; to this, it is replied: "This indeed is the *hari*s; this indeed is the ten, the thousands, the many, and the infinite," because of the infinity of the distinctions among living beings.
What need is there for much? This very Brahman is that Self.
It is "without prior" (apūrva), because no cause prior to it exists; it is "without posterior" (anapara), because no effect subsequent to it exists.
Because there is no other state of being (jātyantara) between them, it is "without interval" (anantara);
likewise, because nothing exists outside of it, it is "not external" (avāhya).
What, then, is that Brahman which is without interval?
This [is known] by itself.
Which one? That which is the inner self—the seer, the hearer, the thinker, the knower, the cognizer, the experiencer of all;
it is the "experiencer of all" because it experiences everything through its entire self.
This is the instruction; this is the teaching of all the Vedāntas.
This is the summarized meaning of all the Vedāntas.
This is the immortal, the fearless.
And the meaning of the treatise is completed. //19//
Thus ends the fifth Brāhmaṇa.
